The internal note is Document 95 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Notes at this level moved paper and policy inside the department while the principals traveled and met. The catalog's older note supplies the date its title omits. The record names the two officials only, and the note's business is in the printed text.
frus-1944-quebec-d195:
White's memorandum for the secretary's files records Morgenthau's morning meeting with Cherwell on September 15, 1944. Cherwell had drafted a summary of the previous day's conversation on Germany policy, the memorandum meant for Churchill. Morgenthau thought it went too far in the wrong direction. It represented, he said, two steps backwards.

Rather than present an inadequate memorandum, Morgenthau argued, they should begin where Churchill had left off and raise the question again that afternoon. The new memorandum should record the new conversation. White also notes a personnel rebuke: Morgenthau told Cherwell that Brand, the British Treasury's man in Washington, was not helping England, and suggested Opie or Keynes instead.
frus-1944-quebec-d295: President Roosevelt received a second message from his secretary of state on 17 September 1944, filed separately as document 295. Like its companion piece from the same day, it sits in the Foreign Relations volume on the 1944 Quebec Conference published by the Department of State. Together the two messages show the department keeping the president supplied with business just after Quebec.
frus-1944-quebec-d95:
Robert Brand prepared a memorandum dated August 14, 1944. Brand represented the British Treasury in Washington. His paper reached the files printed in the Quebec 1944 volume. Britain's finances depended heavily on American support by then.

A Treasury envoy in Washington dealt daily with American officials. His memoranda explained British needs and British limits. Money questions would sit high on the Quebec agenda. They included continued aid and the costs of the Pacific war. For readers, Brand's paper shows the financial case being prepared early. London stated its position a month before the leaders met.
frus-1945-50-intel-d195:
The memorandum of 21 April 1947 is the work of the Acting Secretary of the National Intelligence Advisory Board (Earman). In the printed Foreign Relations series it is document 195, in the volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. At the time, a new National Intelligence Authority oversaw central intelligence, and the Central Intelligence Group did its daily work.

Such notes moved business along: they told a busy reader what had happened, what it meant, and what should come next. Kept in sequence, such memos form the true diary of the office that sent them. Kept with its neighbors in the volume, it shows the new system being built one dated paper at a time.
frus-1945-50-intel-d295:
The Chief of the Special Procedures Group (Cassady) addressed a memorandum to Director of Central Intelligence Hillenkoetter on 30 June 1948. In the printed Foreign Relations series it is document 295, in the volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. By then the National Security Council met often, and questions about secret operations abroad were moving to the center of its work.

A memo of this kind was the basic tool of office work at the top. It put a matter before a senior man and asked for a choice, a signature, or a view. The note's brevity hides its weight: men at this level did not write to each other for practice. Alone it is a page; in sequence it is evidence of how a state taught itself a new trade.
frus-1945-50-intel-d395:
Shane MacCarthy sent a short internal note to J. Prichard Childs on 24 August 1949. Childs led the CIA staff that planned and coordinated intelligence work across the government. The note survives as document 395 in the Foreign Relations volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

Notes at this staff level were where broad policy turned into daily tasks. Childs and his team tried to get the armed services and the civilian agencies to pull in one direction. The note gives readers a ground level view of that hard, plain work inside the early CIA. The volume prints the note in full, with its date and office marks kept as found.
frus-1945-50-intel-d95:
Assistant Secretary of War McCloy wrote to General Magruder of the Strategic Services Unit on 26 September 1945. The volume here opens its thread on the SSU, the War Department's remnant of the OSS. Foreign Relations of the United States prints it in the later volume covering American intelligence between 1945 and 1950.

McCloy had been the OSS's friend inside the War Department since the war, and his protection mattered to the remnant's survival. His letter to Magruder, days after the dissolution order, set the tone of the unit's new life: smaller, quieter, and under watch. Readers starting the SSU thread should note the pairing. Patron and chief, writing across the divide between a great department and a shrinking unit, kept the remnant alive by steady paper.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d195:
Churchill reported his Paris triumph to Roosevelt on 16 November 1944. His message number 822 is printed here in excerpts, in the Malta and Yalta volume. It describes the visit to de Gaulle days after the French capital's liberation season. Half a million French, he says, received him on the Champs Élysées.

He had also patched up his private relations with de Gaulle, who seemed the better for losing much of his inferiority complex. French press talk of grand decisions in Paris was wrong; anything weighty was settled only subject to the three great powers, and above all to Roosevelt. De Gaulle's questions showed how little Paris knew of allied decisions. What he wanted most was modern equipment for eight more divisions, which only America could supply.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d295:
Some Malta meetings left no paper behind, and this short editorial note says so honestly. Printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, it covers a meeting whose substance the editors could not recover. No record of what was said has been found, they state at the outset.

What can be told comes from Churchill's own account, at page 343 of his war memoirs. The note gives the meeting and its participants from that source. It adds one setting detail: Churchill had his quarters in H. M. S. Orion, in Grand Harbor, Malta, during the conference days. The note is a reminder about this heavily documented summit. Even it has gaps that no archive could fill, and the editors chose to mark the gap rather than hide it.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d395:
Hiss's notes of February 8, 1945, run behind the scenes before they reach the plenary. A subcommittee met after lunch — Jebb, Gromyko, and Hiss — to debate procedure for the United Nations conference. Hiss explained the State Department's views, with a caution: the President had not approved them. Stettinius then cleared everything with Roosevelt before the session.

At the plenary, Eden reported for the foreign ministers. He repeated that the next ministers' meeting might be held in London. He explained the invitation rule: states already members should be invited, lest nations join the United Nations just to get invited. Hiss caught the wiring beneath the ceremony.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d495:
Unfinished frontiers are Eden's parting business in this letter to Molotov, written at Alupka on February 11, 1945. Lack of time, he writes, left a few questions unconcluded at the Crimea Conference. Two are named: the Austro-Yugoslav frontier, and the Italo-Yugoslav frontier in Venezia Giulia. Molotov had kindly undertaken to study the British papers circulated on February 10.

On Austria, Eden notes American doubts about his proposal's wording. He attaches a redraft and asks Molotov to substitute it for the paper in his possession. A third matter follows: the British attitude toward a pact between Yugoslavia and Bulgaria. The letter keeps three border files alive past the conference's close.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d95:
Who would sit on the Security Council? A briefing book paper headed “Composition of the Security Council” answers with the Dumbarton Oaks plan. It was prepared for the President's trip and is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume of Foreign Relations.

The Council would have eleven members. Five hold permanent seats: the United States, Britain, the Soviet Union, China, and, in due course, France. Six more states are elected for two-year terms and cannot be re-elected at once. The paper adds that France has now met the terms for its seat, by winning recognition and signing the United Nations Declaration. It also warns that Britain may seek semi-permanent seats for the middle powers.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d195:
John Hickerson passed on Secretary Byrnes's doubts about two British agenda items in a letter dated July 7, 1945. The letter to British Minister Balfour is document 195 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. London had proposed that the leaders discuss posts in the United Nations Preparatory Commission and the seat of the world organization.

The Secretary questions whether these subjects are important enough for the three heads of government, Hickerson writes. Byrnes feels the matters might well be left for solution at the Executive Committee meeting. The short rebuff shows Washington guarding the summit's time for Germany, Poland, and Japan, and treating the new world body's housekeeping as work for a lower level.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d295:
Stalin answered Truman on June 23, 1945, about restoring diplomatic relations with four former enemy states: Rumania, Bulgaria, Hungary, and Finland. Truman's message of June 19 had said the question was still under study. Stalin replied that he noted that fact, but he held to his earlier view.

Nothing, Stalin wrote, could justify any more delay in restoring relations with Rumania and Bulgaria. The short note, sent in translation, marks a clear split between the allies weeks before Potsdam. Washington wanted change in those Soviet-run governments first; Moscow wanted ties restored at once, on its own terms.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d395:
Justice Jackson's report on war crimes questions is summarized in a briefing paper of July 7, 1945. The British government had suggested that war criminals be discussed at the Big Three meeting. Jackson, the American chief prosecutor, cabled on July 4 with the state of the four-power talks on punishing the Axis leaders.

Britain and France, Jackson reported, stood in substantial agreement with the American proposals. The Soviets had answered with a counterproposal that seemed to reject their substance. Moscow wanted many trials under Soviet procedure, mostly on Soviet-held territory, instead of one main trial at Nuremberg. Jackson was unsure agreement would come, but he called it by no means hopeless.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d495:
General Anders's blunt refusal is reported in Kirk's top secret cable from Caserta of June 30, 1945. Broad, the British officer, had lunched with Anders at his headquarters the day before, and talked along the lines of his Foreign Office instructions. Anders listened most politely, and thanked him for the trouble of the call. Then he asked forgiveness for speaking frankly.

Neither he nor his troops, Anders said, could possibly accept as a genuine Polish government the so-called government recently set up in Moscow. They had no illusions about the Russian game. The only responsible, honest Pole in that group, in his view, was Grabski, aged eighty. His tolerance, the cable's end suggests, had limits: no agents of the new government among his troops.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d595:
Minutes of the Secretary's Staff Committee meeting of July 7, 1945, form document 595 in the Potsdam papers. The top secret extract records a 9:15 a.m. session in Washington, chaired by Acting Secretary Grew. The urgent business was the terms of a Japanese surrender.

Grew told the group that a joint Allied statement had been finished on July 6. President Truman had charged him to draft it with the War and Navy chiefs, and Byrnes took it to Berlin. Grew argued that the throne could not in fact be abolished, and that Japan's military machine bore the blame for the war. MacLeish countered that the military had used the throne to control the people. Acheson asked why the military then fought so hard to keep it. Legal adviser Hackworth was asked to draft a short formula for the next meeting.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d695:
Turkey's prime minister told Ambassador Wilson of his disappointment in person on July 3, 1945. Wilson's top secret priority wire from Ankara is document 695 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. Prime Minister Saracoglu had received Washington's cautious reply of June 23.

Saracoglu said he could not grasp Washington's hope for further talks marked by mutual respect. He could not believe the U.S. wanted Turkey to keep talking about ceding bases and land. He took some comfort from the U.S. faith that neither side would breach the new security body's principles. Wilson reminded him that Washington felt the June 7 talk should not be overstressed on the summit's eve. The prime minister answered with a line Wilson quotes in full. Turkey's single problem, he said, was one of life or death, and if the Soviets struck at its independence, Turkey would fight.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d95:
General Deane explained a day of silence from Moscow in a telegram to General Bradley on June 25, 1945. The message is document 95 in the Foreign Relations volume on Potsdam. The Americans had asked to enlarge General Parks's party in Berlin and start the communications work, and no Soviet answer had come.

Deane reports that he handed the request to General Antonov the moment it arrived on June 23, while Harriman took it to Vyshinsky at the Foreign Office. But June 24 was a victory celebration in Moscow and no work was done. Despite constant pressure, no reply had yet come. He promises to keep using every means at hand to win approval for the signal crews.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1095:
Edwin Pauley wrote to President Truman on July 18, 1945, urging him to pin Stalin down on reparations from Italy. Stalin had raised the subject the day before. Pauley wants a clear picture of what the Soviet leader actually expects to take, and how large a sum he has in mind.

Italy, Pauley stresses, will depend on America for sheer survival this winter. Her economy stands near complete disorganization. Estimates of the relief America must ship in by spring run from 500 million dollars to over a billion. Any reparations squeezed from Italy would in truth be paid by American taxpayers, he argues. Goods cannot be shipped out while relief pours in.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1195:
Staff of the British Chiefs of Staff wrote this memorandum on 22 July 1945. The British chiefs produced their own papers for the London team, matching the American series. Their notes gave the British side the armed forces' formal view of the summit's questions.

A British staff paper inside an American volume shows how closely the two allies shared their work. The Western teams planned jointly even when they argued. This memorandum is the British uniformed voice in the record. It lets readers compare how London's soldiers framed the same choices that Washington's staff was framing across the hall.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1295:
The Joint Chiefs of Staff wrote to the State-War-Navy Coordinating Committee on 16 July 1945. That committee was the standing body where the foreign, war, and navy departments meshed their policies. A note to it joined the summit's work to the machine that ran joint policy at home.

The chiefs wrote on the eve of the conference. Their message fed the military view into the committee that would handle much of the follow-through. This paper shows the home machinery being geared to the talks before they began. It is the sound of a government aligning its parts for a fortnight of decisions.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1395:
Jefferson Caffery, the American ambassador in France, wrote to Georges Bidault, the French foreign minister, on 31 July 1945. The volume prints six Caffery letters to Bidault from the turn of August 1945.

Ambassadors do not often write this often to a foreign minister unless the business is both close and pressing. France had been shut out of Potsdam, and Bidault pressed French claims through every open channel. Caffery, in Paris, was the chief of those channels. This letter opens the run, and readers can watch a formal alliance being worked by hand. Paper passed between two men who needed each other, at the hour the great powers settled Europe without France in the room.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-95:
American and British service chiefs met together at Potsdam, and these minutes record their joint session of July 24, 1945. The body was the Combined Chiefs of Staff, the top joint military staff of the two allies. It had run the shared war effort since 1942. Its Potsdam sessions dealt with the war still being fought against Japan.

Joint minutes show two staffs working as one team. They weigh plans, forces, and command questions in shared terms. Readers can trace how military advice reached both governments at once. The record sits in the second Potsdam volume, beside the records of the Big Three themselves.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d795:
Schoenfeld reported from Hungary to the Acting Secretary of State on July 16, 1945, in document 795. The American representative in Budapest wrote on the eve of Potsdam. Hungary sat under an armistice regime, watched by an Allied commission. His report joined the second Potsdam volume beside his opening-day letter.

Two Schoenfeld reports frame the conference's start. He wrote as the talks opened, knowing Hungary's fate would be argued there. Readers see a small post making its case to be heard. The document shows the reach of a summit's shadow: even before it began, its agenda stirred reports from every capital it touched.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d895:
The United States Chiefs of Staff issued this secret memorandum, numbered C.C.S. 706/14, on July 17, 1945. It concerns the disposal of enemy war materiel in Germany and Austria. The chiefs ask the Combined Chiefs of Staff to approve two draft messages attached to an earlier paper, with changes.

One message would let the London Munitions Assignments Board hand captured German gear to forces fighting Japan. The board could assign surrendered or captured materiel held by British or American commands. Until the Control Council agrees on a policy, surplus materiel should not be destroyed. Destruction is allowed only where safety requires it.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d995:
Covey Oliver cabled Seymour Rubin, his division chief, on July 27, 1945, about the planned warning to Switzerland on German assets. The American legation in Bern warns the move may backfire. A formal demand, it believes, would cool Swiss help in tracing and disclosing German property. Unlike Spain, Switzerland shows little risk of assets being drained away.

Oliver asks Rubin's view, based on his Bern visit. He recounts recent talks with the Swiss chargé over Scintilla, a firm with majority German stock. Deletion from the blocked list was refused until Allied rights over the German shares are settled. Oliver suggests Rubin reply to the Department only, to avoid confusing the missions.
frus-1961-63v10-d95: A 1961-1963 FRUS memorandum from the Cuba volume. The Havana file grew. This document holds that memo. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
gao-gaoreports-b-296195: U.S. Reconstruction and Development took its June 2005 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Every challenger gets the full fair-play hearing.
gao-gaoreports-b-298195: The Severson Group took its June 2006 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Every challenger gets the full fair-play hearing.
gao-gaoreports-b-305095: The Chemical Safety Board's membership fees got a fiscal ruling in this December 2005 GAO call, which tests the fee payments. The decision reads the money law. The ruling decides whether the fees were legal. The law had the final word.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-195: Equal opportunity rules in federal workplaces got a GAO explainer in 2005, and the report lays out the policy framework and the roles of EEOC and OPM. The review maps who does what. The workers deserved the clarity. The framework was laid bare.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-495: Bowel disease disability claims needed better SSA help in 2005, and GAO's report says actions could enhance assistance to claimants. The findings demand the aid. The report warns that the suffering deserved support. The actions had to be taken. The suffering deserved support.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-195: Student loan bundling got a GAO study in 2006, and the report weighs what forcing the 2006 loans through one channel would do. The findings do the math. The report warns that the borrowers deserved honest analysis. The borrowers deserved honest analysis.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-295: The border's electronic eyes needed a second look in 2006, and GAO's report says the open questions earned the program a review. The findings demand the rethink. The report warns that the gadgets should prove their worth. The electronic eyes needed honest assessment.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-395: AIDS prevention funding faced a spending rule snag in 2006, and GAO's report says the requirement complicated allocating the emergency plan's dollars. The findings detail the bind. The report warns that the life-saving money needed flexibility. The rules should not block the rescue.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-495: Online SSN sellers rarely had full numbers in 2006, and GAO's report says internet resellers provided few complete SSNs, though Congress should consider standards. The findings test the market. The report warns that the nine-digit keys deserved locks. The standards had to be considered.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-595: The EPA's health risk assessments were getting better in 2006, and GAO's report says steps had strengthened the process, though planning needed work. The findings balance credit and prodding. The report warns that the science behind the rules deserved rigor. The process had to be strong.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-795: Bomb-sniffing machines needed better upkeep in 2006, and GAO's report says the watch over the service deals could improve. The findings target the repairs. The report warns that the airport guards needed steady care. The sentinels needed steady care, and the contracts needed watching.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-95: Tribal environmental requests needed faster EPA review in 2005, and GAO's report says the agency should cut the wait for tribes managing programs. The findings demand the speed. The report warns that the tribes deserved timely answers. The review time had to shrink.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-995: Air Force commercial buying carried risks in 2006, and GAO's report says efforts were needed to address the acquisition dangers. The findings target the exposure. The report warns that the off-the-shelf deals needed harder looks. The risks had to be managed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1195: GAO's 2007 Iraq report card kept flunking the locals: most political, security, and economic benchmarks still unmet. The findings — issued as the surge debate raged — put official optimism on trial. The report's cold numbers asked the hottest question in Washington: was progress real, or just well-spoken?
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-195: Reservists' new health benefits needed explaining in 2007, and GAO's report says the expanded TRICARE eligibility brought educational challenges. The findings target the information gaps. The report argues the part-time troops deserved full-time clarity. The citizen-soldiers earned clear answers.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-95: The White House's management scorecard got a GAO review in 2007, and the report examines the improved financial performance grading process. The findings grade the grader. The report shows the president's report card was itself being graded. The scores had to be fair.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-195: This 2008 GAO report takes a hard look at forest Service: Better Planning, Guidance, and Data Are Needed to Improve Management of the Competitive Sourcing Program. Congress relies on GAO for straight fact-finding on federal programs. Its conclusions can shape how agencies run their programs.
garland-rose-dutchers-coolly-1895:
Stone and Kimball issued Rose of Dutcher's Coolly at Chicago in 1895. Chapter heads trace Rose from childhood and child-life, pagan free, through dangerous days. She meets Dr. Thatcher, leaves home, and enters Madison for study.

Later chapters bring quiet years of growth, a study of the stars, and gates opening wide. Rose reaches Chicago, wins her first success, and sets her face toward the open road. Garland shaped the tale for the farm girls of the West, by his dedication. A woman claims schooling and a writing career against all custom, which made the novel bold for its day.
hardy-jude-1895:
Thomas Hardy published Jude the Obscure in 1895, his last novel, about a stonemason with scholarly dreams. Jude Fawley teaches himself Latin and Greek while working in villages. He hopes to enter the university at Christminster, modeled on Oxford. The doors stay closed to a working man.

Jude's love for his cousin Sue Bridehead defies the rules of church and state. Their life together brings children, poverty, and a grief almost too hard to bear. Hardy attacks barriers of class and marriage law head-on. The book drew such hostility that he gave up novels for poetry. It is his darkest and boldest work of fiction.
hearne-journey-hudsons-bay-1795:
Samuel Hearne, a Hudson's Bay Company man, walked to the Arctic Ocean between 1769 and 1772. His Journey from Prince of Wales's Fort appeared in 1795, after his death. He was the first European to reach the Arctic coast of America overland.

Two attempts failed before the chief Matonabbee led him on the third. Hearne crossed the Barren Grounds, reached the Coppermine River, and saw the northern sea. He also witnessed the massacre of Inuit at Bloody Fall, which he records with horror. His natural history notes on northern animals stayed standard for years. The book is a founding text of Canadian exploration.
herbart-science-education-1895:
Johann Friedrich Herbart published his Allgemeine Pädagogik, General Pedagogy, in 1806, and Henry M and Emmie Felkin translated it as The Science of Education. Herbart, Kant's successor at Königsberg, aimed to do for education what no one had done: deduce it as a science, from ethics and psychology together.

Ethics sets the aim, the formation of character and virtue in the pupil. Psychology supplies the means, showing how ideas enter, combine, and grow in the child's mind. Herbart's watchword is many-sided interest, a mind opened on many sides by good teaching. The book founded scientific pedagogy, and teachers' colleges taught from it for a century. Its order and ambition still impress.
history-of-the-decline-and-fall-of-the-r: The closing volume of Gibbon's history in this edition: the long twilight of Byzantium, the Ottoman conquest of 1453, and the author's famous farewell to thirteen years of labor. Few endings in literature match its melancholy grandeur. The capstone of the greatest history ever written in English.
how-to-read-character-a-new-illustrated-: How to Read Character, 1895. Another edition. This book preserves that manual. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
jataka-cowell-vol1-1895: Volume one of the Jataka tales, the Buddha's birth stories translated by E. B. Cowell. These fables teach moral lessons through the Buddha's past lives. This edition preserves those beloved Buddhist tales. Its contents inform the historical record.
jataka-cowell-vol2-1895: Volume two of the Jataka, continuing the Buddha's birth stories. More tales of the Bodhisatta's former lives in animal and human form. This edition preserves those classic Buddhist fables. The library keeps the document safe.
jewett-life-of-nancy-1895:
Story gathering The Life of Nancy bears copyright dates of 1890 and 1895 in this Houghton Mifflin printing. The title tale leads a list that includes Fame's Little Day, A War Debt, and The Hiltons' Holiday. A Winter Courtship and All My Sad Captains close the contents.

The title story follows a New England girl as she comes of age. Other tales return to Jewett's coastal villages, with strong women, old sailors, and small town rituals. Her touch stays light even when the subjects turn sad. Many judges call Jewett the finest American short-story writer of her generation, and this volume shows her at full power.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mai-johann-hein:
Johann Heinrich Mai the elder, a German Protestant theologian, is included in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia for his work on Judaism. Born in Pforzheim in February 1653, he became a professor at the University of Giessen in 1689. He died at Giessen in September 1719. His writings joined Bible study to Jewish learning.

The article lists the works that earned him his place. Beyond biblical studies, he wrote a survey of Jewish theology, printed at Giessen in 1698. Another work treated the law of the seventh year, the Bible's sabbatical year. His Rabbinic Grammar appeared in 1710. The entry also covers his son, Johann Heinrich Mai the younger. The son taught Greek and Oriental languages at Giessen from 1709. He published a study of Isaac Abarbanel's life and writings, and turned one of Abarbanel's works into Latin. Together the entries record a Christian scholarly family's debt to Jewish texts.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mekilta-de-rabb:
Mekilta de-Rabbi Shim'on is a halakic midrash on Exodus from the school of Rabbi Akiba. Isidore Singer and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach reconstruct it in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. No Talmud mentions it. Medieval writers knew a work they called the Mekilta of Simeon ben Yohai, or simply “the other Mekilta.” They quoted it, Nahmanides often; but apart from scattered citations and one extract printed at Wilna in 1844, the book itself was lost.

The article recounts the detective work. Zunz mistook it for a cabalistic work, and others dissolved it into the better-known Mekilta of Ishmael. Friedmann argued in 1870 that a separate Simeon midrash had really existed, and a geonic responsum published by Harkavy confirmed him. A passage it quotes matches one Nahmanides drew from the Mekilta of Simeon. The entry is thus the biography of a book that survives mainly in the footnotes of other men.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-merech-10695:
Merech, a Russian town in the government of Wilna, is given a short Jewish history by Herman Rosenthal and A. S. Waldstein in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Its Jews enter the record in 1539 through a lawsuit, a debt dispute adjudicated on July 8 of that year. The dispute was between a Jew named Konyuk and a Christian. Twelve years later the Jews of Merech appear again. They are named among the towns exempted from the special tax. That tax, the Serebshchizna, was voted at the Polish diet of Wilna in 1551.

There the early record ends, and the article's second half belongs to the nineteenth century, when the small town produced noted Hebrew scholars. Among them were Mordecai Melzer and Isaac ben Elijah Margolis, who died in New York in 1887. His son was Max Margolis of the University of California. The sources are the Russian-Jewish registers of documents and inscriptions.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-michigan-10795:
Michigan's Jewish history, as Cyrus Adler and Leo M. Franklin tell it in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906, starts late: no records of Jewish settlement before 1848. That year about a dozen Bavarian Jewish families settled in Detroit. Some of them soon pushed north to the copper country of the upper peninsula, peddling in the mining districts.

The state's first Jewish organization, the Beth El Society, became Detroit's Congregation Beth El, founded on September 22, 1850, by exactly the ten men needed for a minyan. Growth stayed gradual, and mostly German, until the Russian immigration of 1883 more than doubled Michigan's Jews and made the newcomers the majority. The article counts at least 65 percent of the state's Jews as of Russian or Polish origin.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moses-ben-isaia:
Moses ben Isaiah ha-Kohen was a Polish rabbi of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. Wilhelm Bacher and M. Seligsohn wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. He was a pupil of Solomon Luria and served in turn as rabbi of Miedzyboz, Brody, and Przemysl.

His printed works are two. Pene Mosheh, issued at Wilmersdorf in 1716, comments on the tales in eighteen treatises of both Talmuds. Karan Or, printed at Zolkiev in 1721, gives homilies that explain two verses of Exodus in fifty different ways. He left other works in manuscript, and some scholars identify him with Moses Wengrow, author of a Haggadah commentary.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mu-ati-moses-be:
Moses ben Judah Mu'ati was a rabbi in Constantinople in the middle of the seventeenth century. The Jewish Encyclopedia entry is credited to its editorial committee and Max Schloessinger. Almost nothing is told of his life. He is known by one book and one responsum.

The book, Yashir Mosheh, printed at Leghorn in 1655 and again at Amsterdam in 1735, comments on the Azharot of Isaac ben Reuben Albargeloni. The Azharot are poems that list the commandments, read on the Feast of Weeks. His single responsum survives inside the responsa of Simon ben Zemah Duran. The notice keeps a Constantinople rabbi's name attached to his work.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nahum-the-mede-:
Nahum the Mede was a tanna of the first century who lived in Jerusalem. The Jewish Encyclopedia article is by its editorial committee and A. S. Waldstein. R. Nathan counts him among the three most renowned criminal judges of Jerusalem. He was one of seven great men of Johanan ben Zakkai's circle who outlived the city's destruction.

He probably sat in the Sanhedrin at Jabneh after the fall. Only six of his halakot survive in the Talmud, and three of them were not accepted. A later sage blamed the rejection on Palestinian dislike of scholars from abroad. The short entry fixes how thin the record of a famous judge can be.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nazarite-11395:
A Nazarite was a person bound by a vow of abstinence. The entry was written by the Editorial Board's Executive Committee, George A. Barton, and Ludwig Blau for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Numbers chapter six sets out the vow's three bans. No wine or grape product may be taken. The hair may not be cut at all. No dead body may be touched, even a parent's.

Samson was the famed Nazarite of ancient Israel. His strength lay in his long, unshorn hair. Samuel, too, was promised under a like pledge. Queen Helena kept the vow for fourteen years. Rich men often paid poor Nazarites' offering costs. Reasons for vows ranged from sickness to a wished-for child. Some rabbis still frowned on such self-denial as sin.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-norway-11595:
Norway forms Scandinavia's northwestern division. Gotthard Deutsch and Josef Wohlstein wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Its people number more than two and a quarter million. The census of 1897 counted over 300 Jews. Their number has since doubled, the entry notes.

A law of 1814 barred Jews from settling there. It dated from Norway's union with Sweden. The poet Wergeland led the fight against it. Repeal came at last in the year 1851. Few Jews used the new right at first. Most who came were from Russian Poland. They hold full civic equality in the land. Trade and industry employ them, mostly with success. Christiania holds the bulk of them today. Its united congregation worships in a rented chapel.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-olshausen-justu:
Justus Olshausen was a German scholar of the East. Crawford Howell Toy and Joseph Jacobs wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Hohenfelde on May 9, 1800. He died at Berlin on December 22, 1882. He read at Kiel, at Berlin, and at Paris.

Olshausen taught the tongues of the East at Kiel from 1830. He lost that post in 1853 for his views on rule. In 1858 he took the same post at Königsberg. He split his work between two great fields. One was Pahlavi, the old tongue of Persia. He did fine first work in that field. The other was study of the Old Testament. His notes on the Psalms, from 1853, made his name.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ostrich-11795:
The ostrich is a great bird that can not fly. Emil G. Hirsch and I. M. Casanowicz wrote on it for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Its Hebrew name in the Bible is bat ha-ya'anah. The bird counts as unclean in the laws of Leviticus. Its name stands in those lists of barred birds.

The Bible tells of its home in lone, waste spots. It tells of its sad cry and its swift run. It tells of its cold heart toward its young ones. Tristram says that charge has some truth in fact. When men come on it with young in tow, it flees. It leaves its chicks to their fate, he says. The Bible calls the bird a fool as well at times. That charge rests on the odd runs it takes when scared.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pappenheim-solo:
Solomon Pappenheim was a German scholar from Zülz, Silesia. Isidore Singer and Meyer Kayserling wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born on February 2, in 1740. He died at Breslau on March 4 or 5, 1814. His father was a help rabbi at Zülz in Silesia.

Solomon became a help rabbi at Breslau in his turn. He is best known for his book on Hebrew word kin. That book came out in three parts in his life. Its name was Yeriot Shelomoh, in the Hebrew tongue. A fourth part of it was left in hand script. His Arba Kosot took its form from Young's Night Thoughts. It was a work in verse-like prose from 1790. He wrote in German in a fight on burial times. He backed the old Jewish use of swift burial in print.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pekahiah-11995: Pekahiah was a king of Israel who followed his father Menahem. Emil G. Hirsch and Schulim Ochser wrote his short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. One chronology puts his reign in 736 and 735 BCE. The kingdom was already breaking apart around him. His chief officer Pekah murdered him in the palace at Samaria. Pekah then took the throne for himself.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-philip-latin-ph:
Two Herodian princes named Philip share this entry. Joseph Jacobs and Schulim Ochser wrote it for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The first Philip was a son of Herod the Great. His mother was Cleopatra of Jerusalem. The second Philip lost his place in Herod's will.

Philip ruled the northeast lands from 4 BCE to 34. His tetrarchy covered Gaulanitis, Trachonitis, and Batanaea. His reign was just, peaceful, and friendly to Rome. He rebuilt Paneas as Caesarea in Augustus's honor. He rebuilt Bethsaida as Julias for Augustus's daughter. His coins first put emperors' faces on Jewish money.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-piyyut-plural-p:
A piyyut is a hymn added to the old liturgy. Gotthard Deutsch wrote the entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The form grew from Talmudic times to the 600s. Its name comes from the Greek word for poetry. The poems still enrich synagogue prayer today.

The oldest piyyutim bear no author's name. Their lines often run in alphabet order. Jose ben Jose is the first named payyetan. Yannai taught Kalir, the most fruitful of all. Saadia followed in the tenth century. Zunz counted over nine hundred such poets. They sang in Spain, France, Germany, and Italy.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-porto-12295:
Porto is the name of an Italian Jewish family with many scholars. Richard Gottheil, Isaac Broydé, and Ismar Elbogen wrote the family article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. First named is Abraham ben Jehiel ha-Kohen Porto. He lived in about the year 1600. He stayed at Cremona, Mantua, and Verona in turn.

At Verona in 1594 Abraham printed a kinsman's book. His own book Hawwot Yair lists Hebrew words in letter order. It gives mystic notes on each word. He wrote a book of poems called Gat Rimmon. He wrote notes on the Pentateuch and the Psalms as well. Those notes were never printed. The article then turns to later members of the house.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-prossnitz-lobel:
Löbele Prossnitz was a false prophet and student of Cabala. Gotthard Deutsch and Henry Malter wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Brody in Galicia late in the seventeenth century. He died in about the year 1750. He moved to Prossnitz in Moravia and wed there.

Löbele earned his bread by peddling in nearby villages. Poor as he was, he lived in a lone, shunned hut. Folk said the hut was haunted by spirits. All at once he took on the role of prophet. He pledged to call down the Shekinah at midnight. A crowd was to watch the glory appear. The entry tells how his trick was staged.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-raudnitz-12595:
Raudnitz is a town in Bohemia with an old Jewish community. Gotthard Deutsch and J. Reach wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Tradition counts it among Bohemia's three oldest Jewish towns. Old tombstones have been found near its former ghetto.

The article says the old cemetery holds over fifteen hundred stones. Many date from the seventeenth century, including martyrs' tombs. A new cemetery opened in 1896. A large temple was built in 1853, with choir and organ. The entry lists rabbis from Nehemiah, who died in 1637. It closes with a 1903 count of four hundred Jews. Readers see a small town with deep Jewish roots.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rossi-azariah-b:
Azariah ben Moses dei Rossi was an Italian physician and scholar born at Mantua in 1513 or 1514. Joseph Jacobs and Isaac Broydé wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. His family traced its line to Jews brought from Jerusalem by Titus.

Dei Rossi mastered Hebrew, Latin, and Italian letters while still young. He also studied medicine, history, archaeology, and church history with rare range. Living at Ferrara in 1571, he survived a deadly earthquake there. In its wake he translated the Letter of Aristeas into Hebrew in twenty days. His own account read the quake as a visitation of God.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sahulah-isaac-b:
Isaac ben Solomon ibn Abi Sahulah was a Spanish scholar and Hebrew poet of the thirteenth century. Isidore Singer and M. Seligsohn wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He is believed born at Guadalajara in 1244.

Sahulah loved poetry and fables from childhood, the entry says. As a man he first gave himself wholly to profane verse. At thirty-seven he changed course and composed his Meshal ha-Kadmoni. It is a set of fables in rimed prose, printed in 1480. He aimed to prove Hebrew as fit for allegory as Arabic. Its five parts treat intellect, penitence, advice, humility, and fear of God.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samuel-baron-de:
Denis de Samuel, later Baron Samuel, was an English financier born in 1782. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Of a Polish family with rabbis among its ancestors, he settled young in Brazil.

At Rio de Janeiro Samuel rose as a merchant with influence at court. Through him the English won leave in 1821 to build a church there. Public Protestant worship, long forbidden, was then allowed in the city. A letter of thanks to him was read in Parliament in 1848. Portugal later made him a baron for eminent services rendered.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schomberg-sir-a:
Sir Alexander Schomberg, a British naval officer, is profiled by Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind in this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906. Schomberg was born in 1716. He died in Dublin on March 19, 1804. He was a younger son of Meyer Löw Schomberg. He entered the navy in November 1743.

Schomberg became a lieutenant of the Hornet in 1747. In 1757 he took command of the Richmond as captain. He then moved to the Diana frigate. In 1760 the Diana helped beat back a French bid to retake Quebec. In 1761 he joined the taking of Belle-Isle under Commodore Keppel. He later commanded the Essex, the Prudent, and the Dorset. In 1777 the lord lieutenant knighted him. For years he headed the list of captains. His Sea Manual of 1789 guided young officers.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-seir-13395:
Emil G. Hirsch, Immanuel Benzinger, Joseph Jacobs, and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906, on Seir. Seir is a region named for Seir the Horite. His descendants held it before Edom's line took over. An Egyptian papyrus of Rameses the Third names the Sa-'a-ira about 1200 B.C. The Bible calls the earlier people Horites, or cave-dwellers.

The mountains of Seir were Esau's home, given him by God. They lie east of the Araba, the rift running south from the Dead Sea. The strip is only fifteen to twenty miles wide. Today it is called Jabal al-Shara. Israel skirted its southern edge on the way north. They avoided entering Edomite land. The tops are bare now, though the name may mean a wooded region. Valleys cut through the range from east to west.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shamgar-13495:
Shamgar, son of Anath, is listed among the judges of Israel in the Bible. Emil G. Hirsch and George A. Barton wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. Judges says he struck down 600 Philistines with an ox-goad. By that act he saved Israel in troubled times.

Deborah's song links Shamgar with Israel's deepest shame. Highways stood empty then, and travelers used hidden paths. Critical scholars doubt the simple picture the text gives. They note his verse looks like a late addition. His name may even be Hittite, and he may have been a foe, not a judge. The entry lets readers weigh tradition against that harder reading.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shi-ur-komah-13:
Shi'ur Komah is a mystic work giving the dimensions of God's body. Wilhelm Bacher and Ludwig Blau wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on it. The work survives only in fragments today. Its largest piece sits inside the book Sefer Raziel.

The measurements are credited to Rabbi Ishmael, the mystic sage. He claimed to receive them secretly from the angel Metatron. God's feet fill the whole world, the text says. Their height runs to countless parasangs, a Persian measure. Each limb bears strange mystic names of its own. Seventy names are listed in the fragment quoted. The entry offers a rare look at bold Jewish mysticism that pictured God in vast, measured form.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-simeon-b-jehoza:
Simeon ben Jehozadak was a Palestinian amora of the first generation of teachers. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. He probably taught Johanan, who transmitted several of his sayings. Those sayings appear across many tractates of the Talmud.

Simeon lived to a very great age, the entry reports. Yannai and Johanan followed his body to the grave. He was a homiletic teacher as well as a legal one. Nearly all his homilies survive through Johanan's transmission. A true scholar does not nurse resentment, he taught. He also warned against appointing men of blameless ancestry to lead. Pride in such leaders could not be checked by shame. Better a Torah letter be set aside, he said, than God's name be publicly profaned.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-skreinka-lazar-:
Lazar Skreinka was a Hungarian scholar who lived in the mid-nineteenth century. Isidore Singer and Isaac Broydé wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He gave his life to teaching. He became principal of the Jewish school founded at Arad by Aaron Chorin. He helped Chorin stir a desire for secular knowledge in that community.

Skreinka wrote a textbook on rabbinic-Mosaic religion and Bible history. It reached a second edition at Arad in 1846. Another work traced the growth of Jewish dogmas and worship. He also wrote essays for Jewish scientific journals. One dealt with the Gnostic principle in the Kabbala. Another explained dark passages in the book of Daniel.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-solomon-of-tour: Solomon of Tours was a French Talmudist and contemporary of Rashi. Wilhelm Bacher and A Peiginsky wrote this brief Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906. The two men carried on a learned correspondence by letter. Rashi addresses him warmly as my dear friend. Rashi also points out an error Solomon made on the Talmud. That frankness proves he was not Rashi's teacher and relative of the same name, whom Rashi revered even in old age.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-staub-hermann-1: Hermann Staub was a German jurist born at Nikolai on March 21, 1856. Isidore Singer wrote this brief Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906. He studied at Breslau, Berlin, and Leipsic, graduating in 1880. Admitted to the bar, he practiced law in Berlin. He made civil law his specialty in that practice. He published commentaries on the German commercial code and on the law of bills of exchange. He also served as associate editor of the Deutsche Juristenzeitung.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-subpna-14095:
A subpoena is a writ that orders witnesses to come and testify. Wilhelm Bacher and Lewis N. Dembitz wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. English law uses the writ to compel attendance in court. Scripture takes a different path to the same end. Leviticus makes testifying a personal duty before God.

Under Leviticus, anyone who saw or heard key facts must speak. Silence left the witness bearing his own iniquity. A party could proclaim his need and curse silent witnesses. Yet rabbinic law gave no earthly penalty for refusing. A baraita lists such refusal among heaven-punished wrongs. Later codes kept that limit on court power. One gloss notes Joseph Caro sought ways to compel attendance. The entry contrasts biblical duty with rabbinic restraint.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sullam-sara-cop:
Sara Copia Sullam was an Italian Jewish poet born in Venice in 1592. Joseph Jacobs and Henrietta Szold wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about her in 1906. Her father Simon Coppio was a cultured, respected man. Sara read Latin, Greek, Scripture, and Spanish in the original. She died at Venice on February 14, 1641.

Sara led a salon prized for wit, music, and verse. Leon of Modena dedicated a drama translation to her. A monk's epic on Esther drew her grateful letter. Ansaldo Cebà then tried to convert her by correspondence. Their letters ran from 1618 to 1622 without moving her. She stayed firm in Judaism throughout the exchange. His letters were printed, but hers were suppressed. The entry honors a poet who held her faith under pressure.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-telesinus-14295:
Telesinus was a Jew of Telesia living at Rome about 480. Isidore Singer and A. M. Friedenberg wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. Pope Gelasius called him a most distinguished man. The pope named him a most deserving friend in a letter. That letter went to Bishop Quingesius of his region.

Gelasius also recommended Telesinus's relative Antonius to the bishop. Papal documents name Telesinus as the pope's physician. Recent writers doubt that medical role, though. Some deny he was a physician at all. The evidence rests on a few papal papers. Berliner's history of Rome's Jews discusses the case. The brief entry weighs a pope's friendship against thin proof. It shows one Jew close to a fifth-century throne of Peter.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tiktin-14395:
Tiktin was a Silesian family of rabbis that came from Tiktin in Poland. Isidore Singer, Schulim Ochser, and M. Seligsohn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Abraham ben Gedaliah Tiktin became chief district rabbi of Breslau in 1816. Only one of his many works reached print.

Gedaliah Tiktin succeeded his father Solomon at Breslau in 1843. Like Solomon before him, Gedaliah championed Orthodox Judaism. He faced Abraham Geiger, leader of the Reform party there. The king confirmed Gedaliah in office despite Reform pressure. He held the post for forty-three years. His charity work touched nearly every local institution. He also visited Jewish prisoners each week. The entry follows a family at the center of a famous feud.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tremellius-john:
John Immanuel Tremellius was an Italian Hebraist born at Ferrara in 1510. Crawford Howell Toy and Joseph Jacobs wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Padua gave him his education. Around 1540 he became Catholic through Cardinal Pole. A year later he turned Protestant and taught Hebrew at Strasburg.

Reformation wars drove him to refuge in England. Archbishop Cranmer housed him at Lambeth Palace in 1547. In 1549 he became regius professor of Hebrew at Cambridge. Later posts took him to Heidelberg and Sedan. He died at Sedan in 1580. His chief work was a Latin Bible from Hebrew and Syriac. Its Old Testament parts appeared between 1575 and 1579. He also wrote a Syriac grammar.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-unna-paul-gerso:
Paul Gerson Unna was a German dermatologist who built a famed skin hospital. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Born at Hamburg in 1850, he took his degree in 1875. He had served as a private in the Franco-Prussian war. That service left him severely wounded.

He assisted Waldeyer at Strasburg after graduation. Dermatology captured his interest in 1881 in Hamburg. He opened a private hospital for skin diseases. In 1884 he founded his well-known hospital at Einisbüttel. A laboratory added in 1887 drew researchers from across Germany. He wrote over one hundred essays in medicine. His journal on practical dermatology began in 1882. Three of his books became standard works.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-vidal-of-tolosa:
Vidal of Tolosa was a Spanish scholar of the thirteen hundreds. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Schulim Ochser wrote this entry. It appeared in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Vidal lived in Catalonia. There he wrote his great work, Maggid Mishneh. It explains Maimonides' code, the Yad, book by book.

Only parts of the commentary survive today. The full work once covered the entire Yad. It was never printed on its own. Printers issued it together with the Yad itself, first at Constantinople in 1509. Vidal also commented in Arabic on a logic work by Al Ghazali. His son Isaac was a scholar too, at Alcala.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wolfkan-of-rati:
Wolfkan of Ratisbon was a Jew who left his faith and turned on the Jews. Isidore Singer and M. Seligsohn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He lived in the last half of the fifteenth century. He is known for his part in a grim court case.

That case was the Simon of Trent affair of 1475. A small boy had been found dead near Trent. Wolfkan said the Jews had most likely killed the child. He claimed they needed Christian blood for the Passover feast. Months later a bishop used that charge at Ratisbon. He accused the Jews there of a like crime eight years past. The entry shows how one man's spite fed a cruel lie. That lie put whole towns of Jews at risk of death.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-yizhak-of-carth: Yizhak of Carthage may be a name born of a scribal slip. Joseph Jacobs and Schulim Ochser wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. One book prints a Greek word in a false form there. That false form looks like a man's name and a town. An editor took it for a sage of Carthage in one note. Bacher held that no such man ever lived at all. The doubt may come from a true Abba of Carthage. That man passed on words in the name of Yizhak.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zebid-15195:
Zebid was a Babylonian scholar of the fourth century of this era. Joseph Jacobs and M. Seligsohn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was a peer of Abaye in the schools of that land. He may have been a pupil of that great man.

He passed on the rules of Abaye, Raba, and Nahman. Yet he held the word of Abaye above all the rest. One grim tale ties that love of his to his death. The men of the exilarch once asked a point of law. A sage gave a rule by the count of two to one. Zebid said Abaye had ruled with the one, not the two. For that word they forced him to drink sharp wine. That draught was the cause of his death, men say. He taught the old bars of Hoshaiah to his boys most of all.
kipling-second-jungle-book-1895:
Rudyard Kipling published The Second Jungle Book in 1895, a sequel to his stories of Mowgli and the jungle. Five new tales follow Mowgli as he grows toward manhood. He faces a drought, a lost city of treasure, and an invasion of wild dogs. Bagheera, Baloo, and Kaa still stand beside him.

The final stories bring Mowgli's farewell to the pack. He must leave the jungle for the world of men, and the parting is deeply felt. Other pieces tell of the far north and of life under the earth. Poems and songs frame each tale. Together the two books form a classic of children's literature.
life-and-death-of-john-of-barneveld-advo:
In Motley's ninth volume, the year 1618 brings open crisis. Prince Maurice sets about revolutionizing provinces he cannot yet control. At Nymegen he claims power to change the town's magistracy at will. Barneveld appeals to the prince and remonstrates with the States.

A libellous pamphlet by Danckaert sharpens the public quarrel. The truce treaty nears expiry as Spain schemes to recover provinces. Motley even reports a secret plot to make Maurice sovereign. The volume ends with the Republic turning against its own chief minister. The Stadholder's visit to Amsterdam marks Maurice's tightening grip. Spain and Archduke Albert watch the expired truce's approach together.
lloyd-etidorhpa-1895:
John Uri Lloyd, a Cincinnati drug maker and writer, brought out this strange novel in 1895. Its odd title is 'the end of earth' writ in a veiled form. Lloyd knew alchemy, old drugs, and the fringe lore of his age at first hand.

A man is led by a guide down through caves to the core of the earth. On the way he learns of odd forces, lost arts, and the deep past of the race. Part tale, part tract on the occult, the book is the classic of its strange kind.
lowell-mars-1895:
Percival Lowell, a rich Boston man who built his own observatory at Flagstaff, wrote this book on Mars in 1895. He had spent a year at the lens in the clear air of Arizona. What he saw on Mars set off a craze in the press of the world.

Lowell held that the dark lines on Mars are canals, dug by a wise race to save a dry world. Melt water from the poles, he said, flows down them to farms and towns. His claim made Mars a lived in world for most lay readers of his age.
mach-popular-scientific-lectures-1895:
Popular Scientific Lectures, published in English in 1895 in Thomas J. McCormack's translation, gathers Ernst Mach's public lectures. Mach, the Austrian physicist and student of science, spoke to lay audiences on the deepest questions of his field.

The lectures take up the economy of thought, the rule that science describes nature in the cheapest adequate terms. They also treat cause, similarity, and the saving of energy in thought. Mach's doubt about atoms and absolutes provoked Einstein's generation of physicists. His style is clear, modest, and quietly radical. These lectures are the friendliest entry into a mind that remade the study of science.
machen-three-impostors-1895:
Three young men of London chase a coin and a conspiracy in Machen's novel of 1895. The Three Impostors weaves its occult plot through the streets and clubs of the city. Tales within tales spin the reader from one strange witness to the next.

Its crown piece, The Novel of the Black Seal, tells of a race of small, evil folk under the Welsh hills. That tale is the direct ancestor of the modern mythos story. The whole book hums with the sense that London floats on an older, darker world. It is Machen's great 1890s romance of evil.
mcclure-s-magazine-december-1895:
McClure's Magazine for December 1895 opens volume six, number one. Ida M. Tarbell edits the lead piece on Abraham Lincoln. Part two takes Lincoln from Indiana boyhood to his first start in life.

Lincoln grew up in Spencer County from 1816 to 1830. Tarbell stresses the sway of his mother and stepmother on the boy. She tells of the flatboat trip to New Orleans and a clerk's post at New Salem. Herndon, she notes, went back in 1865 to save what old friends still recalled. That care for small facts marks Tarbell's whole life of Lincoln. Home sway, not school, did most of the early shaping here.
memoirs-of-the-court-of-st-cloud-being-s:
Volume four of the St. Cloud letters opens at letter thirty three. The writer dates it from Paris in August 1805. Napoleon the First's Italian subjects lead this letter's report.

Their welcome at Milan was cold, not cordial, the writer says. Police agents went ahead to drum up cheers for the coronation. Napoleon blamed England and Russia for the cool mood he found. Strict orders went out to watch all strangers at the rite that day. Pitt and Markof drew his wrath for that cold welcome. Fear of plots sits under the pomp of the Italian crown rite.
mermaid-wonder-wonders-liverpool-1795:
A cheap chapbook printed at Liverpool in 1795 tells of a mermaid met on the Black Rock. Its proud title, The Wonder of Wonders, was the style of such small prints. The tale is the same John Robinson tale told at Whitehaven five years later on.

Robinson, adrift and near death, meets the maid of the sea, who speaks a dark forecast. The folk read his death soon after his home port as the proof of her words. The Liverpool print is the first form of a tale that ports passed from hand to hand.
mikhailowski-shamanism-siberia-1895:
V. M. Mikhailowski wrote this survey of shamanism in Siberia and in the Russian part of Europe, and Oliver Wardrop turned it into English in 1895. It ran in the Journal of the Anthropological Institute in London. At that time few in the West knew the word shaman at all.

The paper pulls facts from Russian reports and sorts them into one clear frame. It tells what a shaman is, how one is called, and what rites and garb mark the role. It was the first English survey to fix the term for the study of faiths.
openalex-w2164028795:
Luciano Canellas and Fábio Olivares published this review in Chemical and Biological Technologies in Agriculture in 2014. They examine how humic substances, dark organic matter from decayed material, promote plant growth. The best-known effects show in roots, which grow larger, branch more, and sprout denser hairs under treatment.

The authors argue the changes reach deep into plant chemistry. Membrane pumps that power nutrient uptake speed up, root secretions shift, and basic metabolism adjusts. Effects vary with environment, plant type, and growth stage, and gene studies disagree in places. They also propose humic matter as a carrier for helpful microbes, a possible new biofertilizer route for sustainable farming.
openalex-w2286459095:
Derrick Fouts, Michael Matthias, Haritha Adhikarla, and colleagues published this study in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases in 2016. They ask what makes a Leptospira bacterium dangerous. The genus spans harmful species, milder ones, and harmless soil dwellers, and leptospirosis is a neglected disease animals pass to people worldwide.

The team compared genomes across all known species of the genus. Family trees show the infectious species split off from the harmless free-living ones. Rebuilt metabolic maps reveal adaptations to life in mammals, including making sialic acid and their own vitamin B12. That self-supplied vitamin appears, for the first time, as a bacterial virulence factor in their analysis.
openalex-w2587566795:
Keith Marion Smith, Carlos Zambrana-Torrelio, and Allison M. White, with colleagues, summarized United States wildlife trade in this 2017 EcoHealth paper. Their aim was to judge the risk that imported wildlife brings infectious disease into the country. They used the federal LEMIS database, the most complete record available. It covers nearly fourteen years of shipments, from 2000 to 2013.

The trade involved eleven billion individual animals and nearly a billion kilograms of wildlife products. Shells and tropical fish made up most specimens, while mammals led shipment counts. Most imports fed the aquatic and pet industries, and a third of shipments held live animals. Most wildlife was reported as wild-caught, with Indonesia the leading legal exporter. Declared shipments doubled over the period. The authors argue inspection and disease surveillance must grow with the trade, since oversight now targets conservation more than disease.
openalex-w2588919095:
Eurídice Martínez Steele, Barry M. Popkin, and Boyd Anthony Swinburn, with Carlos Augusto Monteiro, published this 2017 study in Population Health Metrics. It asks whether ultra-processed foods drag down the overall quality of American diets. Earlier studies had looked at single nutrients one at a time. This team judged the diet as a whole.

They analyzed food records from over nine thousand people in a national health survey. Foods were sorted from unprocessed to ultra-processed, and diets grouped by the ultra-processed share of energy. As that share rose, fiber, potassium, and several vitamins fell, while added sugar and saturated fat climbed. Overall diet quality showed a clear dose-response decline. The pattern held after adjusting for income, education, and other social factors. The authors conclude that cutting ultra-processed foods is a rational way to improve American diets.
openalex-w2808299095:
Sylvaine Giakoumi, Jennifer McGowan, and Morena Mills lead twenty-one conservation scientists revisiting marine protected areas in Frontiers in Marine Science in 2018. Over fifteen thousand protected areas now cover about seven percent of the ocean. They can deliver ecological, economic, and social benefits under the right conditions. Yet failure gets far less study than success, the authors argue.

The group drew on first-hand knowledge of twenty-seven protected area case studies worldwide. They critically examined how success and failure are defined and measured. Focusing on ecological outcomes, where evidence is richest, they find definitions themselves drive verdicts. Expensive protected areas absorb scarce conservation money, so honest accounting matters. Learning from failure is essential to improving practice, they conclude. The perspective asks the field to treat its disappointments as data, not embarrassment.
openalex-w3103836095:
Valeria Piñeiro, Joaquín Arias, Jochen Dürr, and colleagues published this scoping review in Nature Sustainability in 2020. It asks how incentives move farmers to adopt sustainable farming practices, and whether those practices deliver real outcomes. Farm systems face rising pressure to feed the world without wrecking the environment.

The team sifted evidence from nearly eighteen thousand papers on incentive programs. Adoption, they stress, is not a simple yes or no: it depends on farm conditions, effort, and support from governments and partners. Programs tied to short-term economic benefit performed in telling ways the review compares across incentive types. The authors map effects on the environment, farm income, and productivity, giving program designers a clearer view.
openalex-w3118048495:
Stephen Nayfach, Antônio Camargo, Frederik Schulz, and colleagues published this tool paper in Nature Biotechnology in 2020. It presents CheckV, a program that grades the quality and completeness of viral genomes assembled from environmental DNA samples. Such draft genomes are often broken fragments.

Fragments and host contamination can skew studies of viral diversity, host range, and core genes. Bacteria have a standard grader, but viruses lack the universal marker genes it relies on. Simple length cutoffs fail too, since viral genomes range from tiny to enormous. CheckV judges each viral sequence against its own family instead. Cleaner grading lets researchers trust the viral catalogs now pouring out of ocean, soil, and gut samples.
openalex-w3156894395:
Nikolina Ban, Cécile Caillaud, Erika Coppola, and colleagues present a joint test of fine-scale climate models in Climate Dynamics in 2021. Twenty-two European groups ran twenty-three regional simulations at about three kilometres of grid spacing. The study checks how well these models reproduce rain and snow, called precipitation.

The team compared the fine models with coarser models and with detailed observations. The fine models matched observed precipitation more closely, most clearly for heavy rain in summer. Their average error for heavy hourly summer rain fell sharply compared with the coarse models. Spread between models also shrank, which makes local climate outlooks more trustworthy.
openalex-w4214898695:
C. Kavitha, Vinodhini Mani, S. R. Srividhya, and colleagues present machine learning models for predicting Alzheimer's disease early, in Frontiers in Public Health in 2022. Alzheimer's is a progressive brain disease that erodes memory and thinking. It has no cure, so catching it early shapes care and medication choices. Diagnosis today is slow, costly, and depends on expert judgement and heavy data collection.

The authors argue that automated systems can judge cases more accurately than human assessment alone. Their models aim to flag the disease at an early stage, before damage grows severe. Such tools could support doctors' decisions and improve patients' quality of life. They could also help health economists plan the costs of long-term care.
openalex-w4392201695:
Kai Chen, Evan de Schrijver, Sidharth Sivaraj, and colleagues project how population ageing will shape deaths from heat and cold. Their study appeared in Nature Communications in 2024. Older people are among the most vulnerable to temperature extremes. Warming alone should raise heat deaths and lower cold deaths. What ageing populations add to that picture was unclear, so the team modelled eight hundred locations across fifty countries.

At each warming level studied, heat-related deaths rise. Between a fifth and a quarter of those deaths trace to population ageing itself. For cold, ageing mostly cancels the benefit of milder winters, leaving a small net rise in deaths. The findings make ageing a central driver in climate health planning, not a side note.
openalex-w4401894695:
Sebastián Moguilner, Sandra Báez, Hernán Hernandez, and colleagues study brain clocks across diverse populations. Their paper appeared in Nature Medicine in 2024. Brain-age models estimate how old a brain looks from scans. Comparing that estimate with real age can reveal faster ageing or early disease.

The dataset covers more than five thousand people, from Latin America and from countries including China, Japan, and the United States. Most earlier brain-age research drew on narrow, wealthy populations. By including groups with very different incomes, education, and environments, the study tests whether brain clocks work fairly worldwide. That matters for spotting dementia risk early in places past research overlooked.
openalex-w7212144095:
Raimundo dos Santos Sousa, Timotio Henrique Silva, and Rozineide Iraci Pereira da Silva ask how to judge growth in the early years of school, with no tests at all. Tests, marks, and ranks still hang over this stage in many rooms. Yet they fit small children poorly. The team read the national curriculum, the stage's own guides, and past work on kind ways to assess.

To assess, here, is not to drop the watch on learning. It is to change its tools and its ends. Sharp watch of play, written notes, and photos can track a child. So can the child's own work, kept in a file, and plain reports in words. The authors ask for clear aims and skilled staff. They also ask for close talk with families, so notes serve the child, not a rank list.
openalex-w7212188695:
Maximiano Guilherme Tenorio Albuquerque leads a team on the sale-driven turn in dentistry in Brazil, and what it does to fair care. Teeth care sits in two worlds at once. One is a trade, with fees and ads. The other is a right for all, held by the public health system. The essay reads past work on the mouth health plan, on who gets care, and on out-of-pocket costs.

The public plan and its smile drive did widen the door to care, the authors grant. They also cut the worst gaps. But wealth still steers who uses care, who can pay, and who can stay in a course of care. Glam shots and social feeds pull some care toward looks and sales. The essay asks where care ends and the market starts, and backs the public system as the guard of fair shares.
openalex-w7213443795:
Bianca dos Reis Gonsalves Pacheco and Ravine Carvalho Pessanha Coelho da Silva reflect on inclusive physical schooling through neurodiversity. Their 2026 article uses a literature review of work from 2018 to 2024. It asks what physical schooling teachers must do so neurodivergent children truly take part.

Physical education can build interaction, participation, and emotional bonds, the authors argue. Teachers must step in when prejudice appears in class. Curriculum content also needs adapting so every pupil can join in meaningfully. Knowing each student's real situation is presented as the starting point. Without that knowledge, inclusion risks staying a slogan rather than shaping daily school experience.
openalex-w7213446995:
Piedley Macêdo Saraiva and colleagues report a community action in Juazeiro do Norte, Ceará, joining two topics. One is ageism and older people's access to digital technology. The other is safe disposal of electronic waste, which can harm health and the environment when dumped carelessly. Their 2026 article follows action research principles.

Activities at a local day centre included a talk, conversation circles, and interactive exercises. A collection bin and a temporary collection system linked to eco-points were also set up. Twenty people took part directly, teenagers and older women together. The authors report stronger empathy, cooperation, and respect for older people's experience after the work.
openalex-w7213778295:
Vinícius Arantes Campos and Allan Gomes Doriguetto pool trial evidence on protein, energy, and muscle in critical illness. Their 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis follows PRISMA guidance and searches PubMed to July 2026. Only randomized trials using ultrasound to measure muscle were pooled, to keep measures comparable.

Higher protein delivery preserved ultrasound-measured muscle mass, with a moderate and consistent effect once high-risk trials were removed. Earlier clinical outcome trials, by contrast, showed no clear benefit. The authors call that gap a split between mechanism and outcome. Muscle is protected on the scan, they show, even while wider recovery gains remain unproven in the trial record.
openalex-w7214196895:
Ravana Rany Marques Batalha leads a team reviewing scientific literacy through interdisciplinary teaching in Brazil. Their 2026 review searches SciELO, a journals portal, and Google Scholar for national work from 2020 to 2025. Twenty open-access productions in Portuguese formed the final corpus.

Interdisciplinary rationality islands and investigative teaching sequences are the main strategies found, they report. Topics such as the COVID-19 pandemic, fake news, and human environmental impact show the power of socio-scientific controversies. Such themes join knowledge areas and build critical thinking together. Interdisciplinarity widens what scientific literacy can do, they conclude, by helping citizens grasp complex problems and interpret information across the boundaries of single school subjects.
openalex-w7214218695:
Natasha Pereira Salimena and Luiza Santos Cardoso Cruvinel reported a single dental case in a 2026 journal article from Brazil. Their patient was a 54-year-old woman who had worn the same poorly fitting upper denture for about fifteen years without regular dental visits. She had developed a firm, nodular growth where the denture rubbed.

Treatment combined hygiene guidance, a break from wearing the denture, and surgical removal of the growth using electrosurgery under local anesthesia. Lab tests confirmed the growth was inflammatory fibrous hyperplasia, a noncancerous reaction to lasting irritation. Healing went well, function improved, and the growth did not return. The case shows why denture wearers need regular checks and timely replacement of worn prostheses.
openalex-w7214381295:
Mateus Paulo Bartolomeu Gaspar and two colleagues studied informal microcredit in Quibala, Angola, for a 2026 article written through the lens of financial mathematics. Local practices called kixikila and zunga let people in the same town save together and borrow outside the banking system. The authors surveyed eighty active members and spoke with twelve women who run these groups.

Their figures show the true yearly cost of informal credit often runs well above bank rates. Yet members still prefer these systems, because access is easy, no bank-style security is asked, and trust among neighbors holds the deal together. Teaching the math of money, such as simple and compound interest, could turn a source of risk into a tool of power. The authors make that argument above all for non-formal schooling in Angola.
openalex-w7220384995:
Ricardo José Acosta Torreani led a 2026 Spanish-language survey of health workers' vaccination status at the Niños de Acosta Ñu children's hospital, covering March and April 2023. Infectious diseases are a real occupational risk for health staff, and vaccination prevents many of them. Two hundred fifty-five workers, mostly women with a median of five years in service, reported their status against COVID-19, hepatitis B, and tetanus through a digital form.

Coverage differed sharply by vaccine. Nearly all workers had a complete tetanus schedule, and a large majority had completed hepatitis B vaccination. COVID-19 schedules were complete in fewer than half, with the rest incomplete, even though most participants reported having had the disease itself. The study documents a workforce well covered against older routine threats but patchily covered against the newest one, a gap hospital managers can target.
openalex-w7220982895:
Victoria Memran and Karina Mayumi Guimarães Nawai reviewed the science on gut microbiota and obesity. The gut microbiota is the community of microbes living in the intestine. Their 2026 article sets out how it may drive obesity and insulin resistance. Recent research points to swelling, metabolism, and blood sugar control.

When the gut community falls out of balance, the state is called dysbiosis. The gut wall can then weaken. Bits of bacteria slip into the blood. That feeds the slow, low-grade swelling tied to insulin resistance. Gut microbes also shape how much energy food yields. They sway hunger hormones, fat storage, and glucose control. Diet, habits, medicines, and personal traits all play a part. So the authors favor combined approaches that keep the gut community healthy.
openalex-w7221012495:
Maria Eduarda Oliveira Santana wrote a 2026 article on forensic dentistry, the branch that puts dental knowledge at the service of the law.
