Writing in Portuguese, she presents the field as a growing specialty that also touches anthropology and the social sciences, and she asks readers to consider its ethical weight and social use.

Teeth and dental records survive fire, decay, and immersion better than most tissues, so they can identify victims and estimate age. Forensic dentists also help in cases of abuse, disappearance, and disputed identity. Santana argues that such work demands exact records, technical skill, and strict impartiality, because its purpose is justice and human dignity rather than treatment.
openalex-w7221071495:
Kate Marshall and six co-authors report laboratory work on redesigned versions of ciprofloxacin, a widely used antibiotic, in a 2026 paper in The Journal of Antibiotics. Bacteria that shrug off standard drugs, above all Staphylococcus aureus, drive their search for compounds that keep working where the original fails.

The team built and tested variants carrying nitrofuran, furan, and spirocyclic parts. Two of them beat ciprofloxacin by more than eight times against a resistant staph strain in the dish. One compound also protected wax moth larvae infected with staph about as well as the parent drug. Gains were strongest against Gram-positive bacteria, and the authors judge the scaffold worth further tuning.
ostwald-outlines-general-chemistry-1895:
Wilhelm Ostwald, the great systematizer of physical chemistry, summed up his field in Outlines of General Chemistry. James Walker translated the second edition into English in 1895, with Ostwald's sanction. The book treats the young science as one connected whole. Stoichiometry, the weighing of reacting amounts, opens the account.

Chemical dynamics and electrochemistry follow, and catalysis receives its share of care. Ostwald writes as a teacher who wants the field's logic made plain. His outlines gave students a charter text for the discipline. Teachers across Europe and America assigned it for years. The volume shows physical chemistry aware of itself as a science. Its structure influenced later textbooks.
peladan-livre-du-sceptre-1895:
Peladan turns occultist as political thinker in Le livre du sceptre, in French from 1895. The book forms the fourth volume of his Amphitheatre of Dead Sciences. Artist-kings and the spiritual government of nations fill its grand design, where beauty, not ballots or bayonets, should rule the peoples of the earth.

The Sar ranks rulers by their service to the ideal alone. Crowns, sceptres, and courts are weighed as works of art here. His politics dream of a hierarchy crowned by genius and faith. The volume raises fin-de-siecle aestheticism to a system of power, a curious mirror of an age tired of counting houses and crowds.
pike-expeditions-coues-vol1-1895:
Zebulon Pike, a young army lieutenant, explored the upper Mississippi in 1805 and the Southwest in 1806, on orders from General Wilkinson. Elliott Coues's 1895 edition of Pike's journals is the standard text. Volume One gives the journals with Coues's dense notes.

Pike seeks the Mississippi's source, treats with Native nations, and reports on the northern fur country. Then comes the southwestern march across the plains toward the Rockies. Coues, a naturalist, corrects Pike's geography and names the animals and plants. Pike's Peak, which Pike saw but never climbed, keeps his name before the public. The edition rescued his papers from a century of garbled printings.
pike-expeditions-coues-vol2-1895:
Volume Two of Coues's edition of Pike's expeditions follows the southwestern march of 1806 and 1807. Pike had crossed the plains to the Rockies in winter, half-starved and ill-equipped for the snow. Spanish territory lay ahead, and his orders were murky.

He builds a small stockade on the Conejos River, where Spanish troops arrest him as a spy or a guest, depending on the telling. The march through Santa Fe and Chihuahua follows in Spanish custody. Pike's observations of New Spain, its troops, trade, and towns, fill the volume. Coues's notes trace every camp and crossing against modern maps.
pike-expeditions-coues-vol3-1895:
Volume Three of Coues's Pike completes the southwestern expedition and adds the appendices. Pike, escorted by Spanish soldiers, crossed Texas to the American border in 1807. His papers had been seized, yet he rebuilt his report from memory and hidden notes.

The volume gives his return route, his tables of distances and weather, and documents on Wilkinson's schemes. Pike's account of Spanish Texas was America's first good look at the province it would later fight over. Coues closes with a life of Pike, who died a general at York in 1813. The three volumes form the classic edition of an American exploring classic.
pinckneys-treaty-1795:
Thomas Pinckney signed the 1795 treaty with Spain at San Lorenzo, settling the young United States' western and southern borders. Spain ruled Louisiana and Florida at the time, and American farmers in the west depended on Spanish goodwill to ship goods down the Mississippi River. The formal name was a treaty of friendship, limits, and navigation.

The terms gave Americans free navigation of the Mississippi and the right to store goods at New Orleans before export. They also fixed the boundary between the United States and Spanish Florida. For frontier farmers, the deal secured the river road to market through diplomacy instead of war.
plaw-104-1-1995:
Public Law 104-1, the Congressional Accountability Act of 1995, was the first law enacted by the 104th Congress, signed January 23, 1995. Its stated purpose is short and pointed: to make certain laws applicable to the legislative branch of the Federal Government, meaning Congress itself.

Title II extends named workplace protections to congressional employees. It covers rights under the Civil Rights Act of 1964, the Age Discrimination in Employment Act, the Rehabilitation Act, and the Americans with Disabilities Act. It also applies the Family and Medical Leave Act, the Fair Labor Standards Act, polygraph protection, worker adjustment and retraining notice, and veterans' employment and reemployment rights. Later titles take up labor relations, safety, and enforcement machinery for those rights.
plaw-104-10-1995:
Public Law 104-10, enacted May 18, 1995 by the 104th Congress, amends the Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act for one corporation: Cook Inlet Region, Incorporated. It adds a new paragraph to section 7(h) of that act dealing with the corporation's Settlement Common Stock.

The amendment lets Cook Inlet Region buy back its own settlement stock from its shareholders, but only under strict terms. The purchase must be authorized by an amendment to the corporation's articles, approved under set voting standards, and each deal needs prior approval from the board of directors. Offers must generally be made on the same terms to all holders, though the board may treat non-village shares differently to recognize their different rights.
plaw-104-11-1995:
New Mexico and Arizona archaeology is protected under Public Law 104-11, the Chacoan Outliers Protection Act of 1995, approved May 18, 1995. It amends title V of Public Law 96-550, the law that designated the Chaco Culture Archeological Protection Sites.

A conforming amendment widens the protected area's description from the San Juan Basin to the San Juan Basin and surrounding areas. The main section then designates thirty-nine outlying sites, as shown on a September 1991 map, totaling about 14,372 acres. The named sites range from Allentown at 380 acres and Andrews Ranch at 950 to Chimney Rock at 3,160 acres, with small sites like Casa del Rio at 40 acres between them.
plaw-104-12-1995:
Public Law 104-12, the Truth in Lending Class Action Relief Act of 1995, approved May 18, 1995, puts a moratorium on certain class action lawsuits under the Truth in Lending Act. It amends section 130 of that act by adding a class action moratorium subsection.

From enactment until October 1, 1995, no court may certify a class in a covered case. The covered cases involve credit secured by a first lien on real property or a dwelling. The credit must come in a refinancing or consolidation, and not under an open end credit plan. The claims must rest on a creditor's alleged failure to include an incurred charge in the disclosed finance charge. They may also rest on a related disclosure error, or on use of the wrong model form for notice of rescission rights. Exceptions for certain alleged violations follow in the text.
plaw-104-13-1995:
Public Law 104-13, the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995, approved May 22, 1995, aims to make federal agencies more responsible and publicly accountable. Its subject is reducing the burden of federal paperwork on the public. It rewrites chapter 35 of title 44, the chapter on coordination of federal information policy.

The new chapter's sections map the system. They cover purposes and definitions, the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs, and the authority of its Director. They also cover federal agency responsibilities, and the submission and approval of public information collections. Further sections provide for hearings on whether a collection is necessary. They also set up a Government Information Locator Service, public protection, and review of agency activities. Consultation with agencies and the public, and the effect on existing laws, close the list.
plaw-104-14-1995:
House committees changed names when the 104th Congress organized. Public Law 104-14, approved June 3, 1995, keeps the statute books pointing at the right ones. It says that references in United States law to a House committee or officer count as references to the one now in place. That applies when the name or jurisdiction changed in that reorganization.

The text then spells out the main mappings for laws enacted before January 4, 1995. Armed Services becomes the Committee on National Security. Banking, Finance and Urban Affairs becomes Banking and Financial Services. Education and Labor becomes Economic and Educational Opportunities. Energy and Commerce becomes simply Commerce. Foreign Affairs becomes International Relations. Government Operations becomes Government Reform and Oversight. More committees follow in the same pattern.
plaw-104-15-1995: Public Law 104-15, approved June 21, 1995, reauthorizes appropriations for the Navajo-Hopi Relocation Housing Program. Its one section amends section 25(a)(8) of Public Law 93-531 by striking the existing run of years, which ended with 1995, and inserting 1995, 1996, and 1997 in their place. That is the whole law apart from its legislative history: the bill was S. 349, reported by the Senate Committee on Indian Affairs, passing the Senate in April 1995 and the House in June.
plaw-104-16-1995: Public Law 104-16, approved June 21, 1995, reauthorizes appropriations for certain programs under the Indian Child Protection and Family Violence Prevention Act. Its single section amends three sections of that act, 409(e), 410(h), and 411(i). It amends each in the same way: striking the words and 1995 and inserting 1995, 1996, and 1997. The authorizations thus run two years longer. The bill was S. 441, reported by the Senate Committee on Indian Affairs. It passed the Senate in April 1995 and the House in June.
plaw-104-17-1995: Public Law 104-17, approved July 2, 1995, extends authorities under the Middle East Peace Facilitation Act of 1994 by about six weeks. Its one section amends section 583 of the Foreign Relations Authorization Act, Fiscal Years 1994 and 1995, striking July 1, 1995 and inserting August 15, 1995 in its place. Nothing else is changed. The bill was S. 962, which passed the Senate on June 23, 1995 and the House on June 29, days before the original date would have run out.
plaw-104-18-1995:
Medicare select coverage is the subject of Public Law 104-18, approved July 7, 1995. Its catalog title states its aim: to amend the Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act of 1990 to permit medicare select policies to be offered in all states, for an extended period.

The act rewrites the effective date subsection of section 4358 of the 1990 act. The amendments apply in fifteen states chosen by the Secretary of Health and Human Services. They also apply in other states that elect them. The period is six and a half years beginning with 1992. The Secretary must also study medicare select by June 30, 1997. The study compares health care costs, quality of care, and access to services against other medicare supplemental policies. It uses age-adjusted survey samples. A determination follows by the end of 1997. It tests whether premium savings failed to appear. It tests whether spending rose significantly, or access and quality diminished.
plaw-104-19-1995:
Public Law 104-19, approved July 27, 1995, carries one of the longest titles in this run of laws. The title is the Emergency Supplemental Appropriations for Additional Disaster Assistance, for Anti-terrorism Initiatives, for Assistance in the Recovery from the Tragedy that Occurred at Oklahoma City, and Rescissions Act, 1995. It makes emergency supplemental appropriations and rescissions for the fiscal year ending September 30, 1995.

Title I is headed Supplementals and Rescissions, and its first chapter covers the Department of Agriculture and related agencies. Early items move money rather than add it. Funds made available in an earlier law and moved to Nutrition Initiatives are moved again, to the Agricultural Research Service. The Food Safety and Inspection Service appears next. It follows the same account-by-account appropriations pattern that runs through the act.
plaw-104-2-1995:
Senate leaders' use of consultants is rewritten by Public Law 104-2, approved February 9, 1995, which replaces section 61h-6 of title 2 in full. The new text authorizes appointments by the Majority Leader, the Minority Leader, the Secretary of the Senate, and the Legislative Counsel of the Senate.

Each leader may appoint and fix the pay of up to four individual consultants. They serve on a temporary or intermittent basis. The daily rate may be no higher than the per diem equivalent of the top pay rate for standing committee staff. The Secretary of the Senate and the Legislative Counsel may each appoint up to two. The Counsel's appointments are subject to the President pro tempore's approval. One consultant per leader may instead be paid an annual rate under the same cap. Spending comes from the Senate contingent fund. The usual annuity offset rules of title 5 do not apply to these consultants.
plaw-104-20-1995:
Salt in the Colorado River is the target of Public Law 104-20, approved July 28, 1995, which amends the Colorado River Basin Salinity Control Act. It authorizes measures to control salinity upstream of Imperial Dam cost-effectively. It adds a basinwide program to the list of salinity control units.

The Secretary of the Interior, acting through the Bureau of Reclamation, shall implement the basinwide salinity control program. He may act directly, or through grants and advances to non-federal groups. The program consists of cost-effective measures and works to reduce salinity from many sources. The sources include saline springs, leaking wells, irrigation sources, and industrial sources. They include erosion of public and private land, or other sources the Secretary finds right. Lost fish and wildlife values must be made up for. Before spending on any measure, the Secretary must send a planning report to the committees of Congress and wait thirty days.
plaw-104-21-1995:
District road projects get federal relief under Public Law 104-21, the District of Columbia Emergency Highway Relief Act, approved August 4, 1995. For fiscal years 1995 and 1996 it temporarily waives the normal non-federal share of costs. The federal share may rise to a percentage the District requests, up to 100 percent of a project's costs.

Eligible projects are highway projects in the District. For them, the United States is already obligated, or becomes obligated by September 30, 1996, to pay a federal share under title 23. The project must sit on a route proposed for or designated as part of the National Highway System. Or it must be of regional significance, as the Secretary of Transportation determines. The District must also certify that sufficient funds are not available to pay the non-federal share. A third section takes up a dedicated highway fund and repayment of the waiver amounts.
plaw-104-22-1995: Public Law 104-22, approved August 14, 1995, extends authorities under the Middle East Peace Facilitation Act of 1994 until October 1, 1995. Its main section amends section 583(a) of the Foreign Relations Authorization Act, Fiscal Years 1994 and 1995. That section had been amended before by Public Law 104-17. The change strikes August 15, 1995 and inserts October 1, 1995. A consultation subsection adds a rule for exercises of the authority before August 16, 1995. For those, the written policy justification dated June 1, 1995 and its consultations satisfy the act's requirements. The bill was H.R. 2161.
plaw-104-23-1995: Public Law 104-23 is the Corning National Fish Hatchery Conveyance Act, approved September 6, 1995. It directs the Secretary of the Interior to convey the Corning National Fish Hatchery to Arkansas within 180 days, without reimbursement. The hatchery will serve the state fish culture program. The hatchery, popularly known as the William H. Donham State Fish Hatchery, sits a mile west of Corning on Highway 67 in Clay County. It covers 137.34 acres, with its buildings and equipment. Misuse triggers reversion to the United States.
plaw-104-24-1995: Public Law 104-24, approved September 6, 1995, directs the Secretary of the Interior to convey a fish hatchery to the State of Iowa within 180 days, without reimbursement. The hatchery will be used for fishery resources work. The hatchery is the Fairport National Fish Hatchery in Muscatine County, Iowa. It sits adjacent to State Highway 22 west of Davenport. It includes all real property, improvements, and personal property. If Iowa uses the property for any other purpose, all right, title, and interest reverts to the United States. The bill was H.R. 584, with House Report 104-35.
plaw-104-25-1995: Public Law 104-25, approved September 6, 1995, directs the Secretary of the Interior to convey the New London National Fish Hatchery to the State of Minnesota. The transfer must occur within 180 days, without reimbursement, despite any other law. The facility sits outside downtown New London. It includes its easements, water rights, land, improvements, and related property. The Minnesota Department of Natural Resources will use it for the state fishery resources management program. Any other use triggers reversion of all title to the United States.
plaw-104-26-1995:
Court reporters working for public agencies are treated differently for overtime under Public Law 104-26, the Court Reporter Fair Labor Amendments of 1995, approved September 6, 1995. It amends the Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938 to exempt employees performing certain court reporting duties from the compensatory time requirements that apply to some public agencies.

A new paragraph in section 7(o) sets the rule. Hours a public agency employee spends on court reporting transcript preparation are not counted as hours worked for overtime purposes. Two conditions must hold. The rate must be at least as high as the maximum set by state law or local ordinance. The maximum may instead be one set by a judicial or administrative officer as of July 1, 1995. Or the rate may be one freely negotiated with the requesting party, other than the presiding judge. And the work must fall outside the employee's other agency hours.
plaw-104-27-1995: Public Law 104-27, approved September 6, 1995, names the United States Post Office building at 33 College Avenue in Waterville, Maine. It is the George J. Mitchell Post Office Building. A references section covers later mentions. Any law, map, rule, paper, or other record that names that building counts as naming the new name. The bill was H.R. 2077. It passed the House on August 4, 1995 and the Senate on August 9.
plaw-104-28-1995:
Public Law 104-28, the District of Columbia Convention Center and Sports Arena Authorization Act of 1995, approved September 6, 1995, clears the way for two Washington building projects. Its table of contents shows three titles, one for the convention center, one for a sports arena, and one waiving congressional review.

Title I permits the Washington Convention Center Authority to spend revenues on operating and maintaining the existing Washington Convention Center. It also permits spending on preconstruction activities for a new convention center. Title II permits a designated District authority to borrow funds for preconstruction activities for a Gallery Place sports arena. It permits certain District revenues to be pledged as security for that borrowing. It also states that no appropriation is necessary for the arena preconstruction work, and describes those activities. Title III waives congressional review of an arena tax payment and use matter.
plaw-104-29-1995:
Lending disclosures are clarified by Public Law 104-29, the Truth in Lending Act Amendments of 1995, approved September 30, 1995. It clarifies the act's intent and reduces burdensome requirements on creditors, starting with which charges count in the finance charge.

Section 2 provides that the finance charge shall not include fees imposed by third party closing agents. The agents include settlement agents, attorneys, and escrow and title companies. The exclusion holds if the creditor does not require the charges or services and does not retain the charges. Borrower-paid mortgage broker fees go the other way: they are included in the finance charge. That holds whether paid in cash or financed, to the broker or to the lender for delivery to the broker. The Federal Reserve Board must issue implementing regulations within six months. That change takes effect sixty days after those regulations or twelve months after enactment, whichever comes first.
plaw-104-3-1995: Public Law 104-3 is a short act from March 7, 1995. It changes the federal charter of the Veterans of Foreign Wars. The change is about who may join the group. Before, a member needed campaign-medal service in a war or expedition abroad. Now a veteran also qualifies through honorable service in Korea. The service must last at least 30 straight days, or 60 days in all, after June 30, 1949. Service in Korean waters counts as well.
plaw-104-30-1995: Public Law 104-30 is a short act from September 30, 1995. It extends powers under the Middle East Peace Facilitation Act of 1994. The old end date was October 1, 1995. The act moves it to November 1, 1995. It also settles a paperwork point. A policy paper sent to Congress on June 1, 1995 counts as meeting the law's consultation step for acts before October 5, 1995.
plaw-104-31-1995:
When the regular spending bills for fiscal year 1996 were not finished in time, Congress passed a stopgap. Public Law 104-31, approved September 30, 1995, makes continuing appropriations for fiscal year 1996, keeping federal departments and agencies funded and running.

The joint resolution provides such amounts as may be necessary to continue projects and activities that were conducted in fiscal year 1995, under the authority and conditions of that year's appropriations acts. It names the pending 1996 bills it stands in for, covering agriculture, commerce, justice, defense, the District of Columbia, energy and water, foreign operations, interior, and labor, health, and education, among others.
plaw-104-32-1995:
The Military Construction Appropriations Act, 1996 became Public Law 104-32 on October 3, 1995. It funds building work for the armed forces for one year. The year ends September 30, 1996. The act also funds family housing and base closures.

Army building work gets more than six hundred million dollars. The money builds and equips bases and other real property. A capped share pays for studies, plans, and design work. Navy building work gets more than five hundred fifty million dollars. The Navy money runs through its facilities engineering command. Both sums stay open for use until September 30, 2000.
plaw-104-33-1995: Public Law 104-33, approved October 3, 1995, is a short act aligning deadlines in a federal court experiment. It amends the Civil Justice Reform Act of 1990 to make the reporting deadlines for studies in federal court demonstration districts consistent with those for pilot districts. The demonstration program period is lengthened from four years to five, and the date in the reporting provision moves from December 31, 1995 to December 31, 1996.
plaw-104-34-1995: Public Law 104-34 is a tiny act from October 3, 1995. It clarifies the rules on venue in federal court. Venue is the place where a case may be filed. The act changes one phrase in title 28. The old text spoke of where the defendants are. The new text speaks of where any defendant is. That one word shift settles how the rule reads when a suit has more than one defendant.
plaw-104-35-1995: Public Law 104-35 is an act from October 12, 1995. It gives states two more years to build a computer system. The system runs state plans for child and spousal support. It must handle data and records for those plans. The act changes one year in the Social Security Act. The old year was 1995. The new year is 1997. A second part makes small fixes tied to the end of federal funding for the work.
plaw-104-36-1995:
The Small Business Lending Enhancement Act of 1995 became Public Law 104-36 on October 12, 1995. It aims to cut the cost of federal loan guarantees. The guarantees back loans and debentures for small firms.

The act resets the federal share in guaranteed loans. For loans over one hundred thousand dollars, the share is seventy-five percent. For smaller loans, the share is eighty percent. A lender may ask for a lower share. But the agency may not use that request to rank loan requests. The act amends both the Small Business Act and the Small Business Investment Act of 1958.
plaw-104-37-1995:
Farms, food safety, and rural programs were funded for one year by the Agriculture, Rural Development, Food and Drug Administration, and Related Agencies Appropriations Act, 1996. Public Law 104-37, approved October 21, 1995, appropriates money for those programs for the fiscal year ending September 30, 1996.

Title I covers agricultural programs, starting with the Office of the Secretary of Agriculture, funded at more than ten million dollars, most of it for the InfoShare system. It also funds executive operations such as the Chief Economist, whose work includes economic analysis, risk assessment, cost-benefit analysis, and the World Agricultural Outlook Board. The act goes account by account through the department's production, processing, and marketing work.
plaw-104-38-1995:
Public Law 104-38 dates from October 30, 1995. Congress used its review power to block new sentencing rules. The blocked rules would have lowered crack cocaine sentences. They also touched sentences for money laundering. A third topic was deals in property gained from crime.

The blocked items were amendments 5 and 18. The Sentencing Commission had sent them to Congress on May 1, 1995. They never took effect. The act then orders new advice on cocaine sentencing. Crack trafficking should draw a longer term than the same amount of powder cocaine. Top-level dealers should get more time than street sellers.
plaw-104-39-1995:
Music was moving onto digital networks in the mid-1990s, and the Digital Performance Right in Sound Recordings Act of 1995 updated copyright law to meet it. Public Law 104-39, approved November 1, 1995, amends title 17 of the United States Code to give sound recordings an exclusive public performance right in digital transmissions.

The act adds a new paragraph to the list of exclusive rights in copyrighted works: for sound recordings, the right to perform the work publicly by means of a digital audio transmission. It then rewrites the section limiting that right, setting out exempt transmissions and retransmissions that do not need permission. Traditional radio had never owed this performance right for recordings; the act created it for the digital setting.
plaw-104-4-1995:
The Unfunded Mandates Reform Act of 1995 became Public Law 104-4 on March 22, 1995. It answers a complaint from states and towns. Washington kept ordering them to act, but sent no money to pay for it.

The act states its goals at the start. It wants a stronger partnership with state, local, and tribal governments. It wants to end mandates set without full thought by Congress. It also wants cost facts ready before votes. So the act sets up a way to size up mandates in new bills. Both houses see those facts before they vote.
plaw-104-40-1995: Public Law 104-40 dates from November 1, 1995. It lets the federal government charge fees for one small service. The service is the inspection of triploid grass carp. Fish farms ask for these checks. The Secretary of the Interior may set fair fees for the work. The Fish and Wildlife Service does the inspections. Fees paid stay with the service. They fund the inspection work itself. No new funding act is needed to spend them.
plaw-104-41-1995:
Public Law 104-41 is a patent act from November 1, 1995. It deals with patents on biotech processes. A process could look obvious just because the stuff it made was new. The act fixes that trap in title 35.

The rule works like this. A biotech process counts as nonobvious if the matter it uses or makes is new and nonobvious. The claims must share one filing date. They must also have the same owner. A patent on the process must hold the claims to the matter as well. Or it must end on the same date as the patent that does.
plaw-104-42-1995:
Public Law 104-42 is an Alaska land act from November 2, 1995. It amends the Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act. That 1971 act settled the land claims of Alaska Natives.

Title I ratifies two land transfers as federal law. Cook Inlet Region, Inc. conveyed land to two village groups. One is the Montana Creek Native Association. The other is the Caswell Native Association. Each group got about eleven thousand five hundred twenty acres. Both groups are deemed to have their full share. No more land is due to them. The act also deals with mining claims on land already conveyed to regional firms.
plaw-104-43-1995:
The Fisheries Act of 1995 became Public Law 104-43 on November 3, 1995. It amends the Fishermen's Protective Act. Its chief part covers United States fishing boats on the high seas.

Title I sets up permits for those boats. It lists acts that are banned on the high seas. It also sets civil fines, permit sanctions, crimes, and forfeitures. The Secretary holds set duties under the title. Title II carries out a treaty on fish in the northwest Atlantic. It covers the United States seat under that treaty. It also covers requests for scientific advice.
plaw-104-44-1995: A Colorado post office gained a name under Public Law 104-44. The act was signed on November 3, 1995. It names the post office building at 201 East Pikes Peak Avenue. The site is in Colorado Springs. Its name is now the Winfield Scott Stratton Post Office. Any federal record that speaks of the building uses that name. The act is a simple naming measure of the 104th Congress.
plaw-104-45-1995:
The Jerusalem Embassy Act of 1995 became Public Law 104-45 on November 8, 1995. It calls for moving the United States Embassy in Israel to Jerusalem.

The act opens with findings. Each nation may name its own capital, Congress says. Jerusalem has been Israel's capital since 1950. It is the seat of Israel's president, parliament, and top court. The city is the spiritual center of Judaism. It is also holy to other faiths. The findings note that the city was split from 1948 to 1967. It was reunited in the Six Day War. Congress had said in 1990 that the city must stay whole.
plaw-104-46-1995:
The Energy and Water Development Appropriations Act, 1996 became Public Law 104-46 on November 13, 1995. It funds energy and water work for one year. The year ends September 30, 1996.

Title I funds the civil works of the Army Corps of Engineers. The Corps builds and studies river and harbor projects. It also handles flood control and beach erosion. One account pays for general studies and surveys. It holds more than one hundred twenty million dollars. Named projects include the Ohio River Greenway in Indiana. Kentucky Lock and Dam also gets a set sum. The act passed as H.R. 1905.
plaw-104-47-1995: Public Law 104-47 is a short act from November 13, 1995. It extends powers under the Middle East Peace Facilitation Act of 1994 once more. An earlier act had set the end date at November 1, 1995. This act strikes that date. It inserts December 31, 1995. A policy paper from June 1, 1995 counts for the consultation step. That rule covers acts before November 14, 1995. Note the act's heading names November 13. The text itself runs to the end of the year.
plaw-104-48-1995:
The Perishable Agricultural Commodities Act Amendments of 1995 became Public Law 104-48 on November 15, 1995. It updates the 1930 act that polices the fresh produce trade. The stated aims are to modernize and strengthen that act.

The act defines retailer and grocery wholesaler for the first time. It phases out the yearly license fee for those dealers. It resets fees for brokers and commission merchants. Fines for trading without a license go up. So does the late renewal fee. Other parts cover the trust on produce and sale proceeds. They also cover complaint fees and the ban on false labels. Civil fines may now replace license loss in some cases.
plaw-104-49-1995:
Public Law 104-49 dates from November 15, 1995. It sorts out two benefit systems for hurt farm workers. One is state workers' compensation. The other is the Migrant and Seasonal Agricultural Worker Protection Act.

Where state comp law covers a migrant or seasonal worker, it is the sole remedy for injury or death. The worker cannot also win actual damages under the federal act. But statutory damages and court orders for fairness stay open. Back pay and front pay are barred. A second part expands statutory damages under the act. The change covers all cases with no final judgment yet.
plaw-104-5-1995: Public Law 104-5 is a one-word act from March 23, 1995. It amends the Elementary and Secondary Education Act of 1965. The part at issue deals with Indian education. Congress had added it in the Improving America's Schools Act of 1994. In one line of that part, the word and is struck. The word or takes its place. Nothing else in the act changes. It is among the shortest laws of the 104th Congress.
plaw-104-50-1995:
Planes, highways, and transit for fiscal year 1996 were funded by the Department of Transportation and Related Agencies Appropriations Act, 1996. Public Law 104-50, approved November 15, 1995, makes appropriations for the Department of Transportation and related agencies for the year ending September 30, 1996.

Title I opens with the Office of the Secretary, funded at more than fifty-six million dollars for salaries and expenses, including money credited from user fees for the electronic tariff filing system. The act also provides about six and a half million dollars for the Office of Civil Rights. Its conditions bar spending to keep custody of airline tariffs that are already publicly available at no cost.
plaw-104-51-1995: Public Law 104-51 is a wording act from November 15, 1995. It updates terms in the Immigration and Nationality Act. The terms sit in the act's definition of child. That definition guides how children are classed under immigration law. The phrase legitimate child becomes child born in wedlock. The phrase illegitimate child becomes child born out of wedlock. The change appears in two spots in the definition. The legal classes stay the same. Only the words for them are new.
plaw-104-52-1995:
The Treasury Department, the Postal Service, and the White House offices were funded for a year by the Treasury, Postal Service, and General Government Appropriations Act, 1996. Public Law 104-52, approved November 19, 1995, covers the fiscal year ending September 30, 1996.

Title I appropriates for the Treasury Department, starting with Departmental Offices at more than one hundred five million dollars. That account covers running the Treasury Building and Annex, official travel, information technology modernization, and a small fund for unforeseen confidential emergencies spent on the Secretary's certificate alone. Part of the money reimburses the District of Columbia Metropolitan Police Department for personnel costs from a defined period in 1995.
plaw-104-53-1995:
Congress paid its own bills for fiscal year 1996 in the Legislative Branch Appropriations Act, 1996. Public Law 104-53, approved November 19, 1995, makes appropriations for the legislative branch for the year ending September 30, 1996.

Title I, the Congressional Operations Appropriations Act portion, begins with the Senate. It sets expense allowances of ten thousand dollars each for the Vice President, the President Pro Tempore, and the majority and minority leaders, and representation allowances for the two leaders. Salaries, officers, and employees of the Senate receive more than sixty-nine million dollars, including about one and a half million dollars for the Office of the Vice President.
plaw-104-54-1995: Public Law 104-54 is a stopgap funding act from November 19, 1995. It is a joint resolution of the 104th Congress. Several spending bills for fiscal year 1996 were still unfinished. The resolution keeps the government funded in the meantime. It grants the sums needed to carry on fiscal year 1995 projects. Loans and loan guarantees are part of that. The pending bills it bridges include defense and foreign operations. It also covers the District of Columbia and the interior bill.
plaw-104-55-1995:
The Edible Oil Regulatory Reform Act became Public Law 104-55 on November 20, 1995. It tells federal agencies to treat food oils apart from petroleum. Rules on oils and greases must now split them into classes.

One class holds animal fats, fish oils, and vegetable oils. The other holds all other oils and greases. Petroleum sits in that second class. Rule makers must weigh how the classes differ. Their traits and their effects on nature both count. The Food and Drug Administration is exempt from the act. So is the Food Safety and Inspection Service.
plaw-104-56-1995: Public Law 104-56, approved November 20, 1995, is a second joint resolution making further continuing appropriations for fiscal year 1996, passed a day after a nearly identical measure. It appropriates such amounts as may be necessary to continue fiscal year 1995 projects and activities, including direct loans and loan guarantees, under the earlier acts' authority. The pending 1996 appropriations bills it stands in for include commerce, justice, and state; defense; the District of Columbia; foreign operations; and interior.
plaw-104-57-1995:
The Veterans' Compensation Cost-of-Living Adjustment Act of 1995 became Public Law 104-57 on November 22, 1995. It raises pay for veterans with service-connected disabilities. It also raises support for their survivors.

The new rates start on December 1, 1995. The Secretary of Veterans Affairs must raise the sums in the pay schedules. The list covers basic disability pay and extra sums for dependents. It covers the clothing allowance as well. Survivor rates rise too, for spouses and for children. Extra sums for young children and for disability are on the list. The act also says how the percent of the raise is set.
plaw-104-58-1995:
Public Law 104-58 dates from November 28, 1995. It joins two Alaska energy measures in one act. One directs the sale of the Alaska Power Administration. The other allows the export of Alaska North Slope crude oil.

Title I is the Alaska Power Administration Asset Sale and Termination Act. It sets up the sale of the agency's hydro power projects. The buyers were set by deals from 1989. Eklutna goes to Anchorage's city power firm and two electric co-ops. Snettisham goes to a state authority. Title II takes up the oil export question.
plaw-104-59-1995:
The National Highway System Designation Act of 1995 became Public Law 104-59 on November 28, 1995. It names the National Highway System in federal law. The system is the network of key highways across the United States.

Title II gives states more room on funds. It covers funding restoration and rescissions. It also covers state balances that sit unused, and relief from mandates. Title III adds highway rules. They treat traffic control on the system and design standards. They also cover call boxes for motorists and limits on advance building. The act passed as S. 440.
plaw-104-6-1995:
The Emergency Supplemental Appropriations and Rescissions for the Department of Defense to Preserve and Enhance Military Readiness Act of 1995 is Public Law 104-6. It was signed on April 10, 1995. It adds emergency funds for the year ending September 30, 1995. It also cuts other funds through rescissions.

Title I holds the new money. Army personnel accounts gain more than two hundred sixty million dollars. The Navy gains more than one hundred eighty million. Marine Corps accounts follow. Each sum is marked as an emergency need. That marking uses the Balanced Budget and Emergency Deficit Control Act of 1985.
plaw-104-60-1995: Public Law 104-60 dates from November 28, 1995. It amends the start rules for some temporary federal judgeships. The judgeships came from the Judicial Improvements Act of 1990. The act swaps the last sentence of that rule. The new rule works like this. In each named district, one vacancy goes unfilled. It is the first vacancy five years or more after the temporary judge was confirmed. For the western district of Michigan, the first vacancy after December 1, 1995 goes unfilled.
plaw-104-61-1995:
The Department of Defense Appropriations Act, 1996 became Public Law 104-61 on December 1, 1995. It funds the armed forces for one year. The year ends September 30, 1996.

Title I pays the troops. The Army personnel account holds nearly twenty billion dollars. It pays wages, allowances, clothing, and travel for moves. It also pays into the military retirement fund. Cadets and aviation cadets are covered. Navy personnel get a like account. It covers sailors, midshipmen, and cadets on active duty. The act is the chief defense funding act for that year. It passed as H.R. 2126.
plaw-104-62-1995:
The Philanthropy Protection Act of 1995 became Public Law 104-62 on December 8, 1995. It helps charities raise funds. It writes some breaks from the federal securities laws into the statutes.

The act amends the Investment Company Act of 1940. It exempts groups run only for religious, charitable, or like aims. Pooled income funds held by a charity are covered too. Collective funds for gifts are also covered. More parts amend the Securities Act of 1933. The Securities Exchange Act of 1934 is amended as well. So is the Investment Advisers Act of 1940. One part guards philanthropy under state law.
plaw-104-63-1995:
Charities commonly set gift annuity payments using the same suggested rates, and the Charitable Gift Annuity Antitrust Relief Act of 1995 made sure that practice was not treated as price fixing. Public Law 104-63, approved December 8, 1995, modifies the antitrust laws, and similar state laws, for charitable gift annuities.

The act provides that it is not unlawful for two or more tax-exempt charitable organizations to use, or agree to use, the same annuity rate when issuing charitable gift annuities. A state may opt out of the shelter for its own antitrust-like law by enacting a statute saying so within three years. The act defines annuity rate as the percentage of a gift's fair market value paid yearly to the annuitants for life.
plaw-104-64-1995: Public Law 104-64 is the Defense Production Act Amendments of 1995. It was signed on December 18, 1995. It extends the Defense Production Act of 1950. That act gives the president powers over industry for national defense. The end date for titles I, III, and VII moves. It goes from September 30, 1995 to September 30, 1998. The act funds title III projects for three years. The sums are those needed for the work. It also tells the president to send reports to Congress.
plaw-104-65-1995:
The Lobbying Disclosure Act of 1995 became Public Law 104-65 on December 19, 1995. It forces paid lobbying of the federal government into the open.

Congress found that the public needs to know what paid lobbyists do. Their work touches both Congress and the agencies. The old disclosure laws had failed, Congress said. Their words were unclear. Their enforcement was weak. No one could tell who had to register or report. The act then defines its terms with care. A client hires or keeps a person to lobby for them. The act sits in title 2 of the United States Code.
plaw-104-66-1995:
Paperwork Congress no longer needed was targeted by the Federal Reports Elimination and Sunset Act of 1995. Public Law 104-66, approved December 21, 1995, provides for the modification or elimination of federal reporting requirements across the government.

Title I works department by department, with paired sections listing reports eliminated and reports modified. It opens with the Department of Agriculture and continues through Commerce, Defense, Education, and Energy, among others. The approach is surgical rather than sweeping: each recurring report owed to Congress is named, then killed outright or trimmed, cutting the flow of unread studies agencies had been required to produce.
plaw-104-67-1995:
The Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995 became Public Law 104-67 on December 22, 1995. It reforms suits over stocks and bonds in federal court.

Title I aims at abusive suits. It rewrites the rules for private securities cases. It adds a safe harbor for forward-looking claims by firms. It also backs the power of the Securities and Exchange Commission to sue aiders. One part treats loss causation. Title II seeks fewer forced settlements. It does so through proportionate liability. Title III tells auditors to detect and disclose corporate fraud. It passed as H.R. 1058.
plaw-104-68-1995: A big federal building in Washington gained a name under Public Law 104-68. The act was signed on December 22, 1995. The building was still under construction at the time. It stands at 14th Street and Pennsylvania Avenue, Northwest. The site is the Federal Triangle Project. Its name is now the Ronald Reagan Building and International Trade Center. Any federal record that speaks of the building uses that name.
plaw-104-69-1995: Public Law 104-69 is a narrow stopgap act from December 22, 1995. It makes further continuing appropriations for fiscal year 1996. Most stopgaps of that season covered the whole government. This one covers two programs only. One is aid to families with dependent children. The other is foster care and adoption assistance. Both run through the Administration for Children and Families. The act funds them at the rate then in effect. It also funds the office work the programs need.
plaw-104-7-1995:
Public Law 104-7 is a tax act from April 11, 1995. It helps self-employed people with health insurance costs. Their deduction for those costs had been temporary. The act makes it permanent.

The deduction applies to tax years after December 31, 1993. The act also raises the share that can be deducted. It goes from twenty-five percent to thirty percent. That change starts with tax years after December 31, 1994. A second part repeals a tax break on some media sales. Those sales had served Federal Communications Commission policies. Related code references are cleaned up.
plaw-104-70-1995:
Public Law 104-70 is a Clean Air Act change from December 23, 1995. It makes employer trip reduction plans optional. The plans cut work trips and miles in bad ozone areas. The areas are those rated severe.

Before, some states had to require such plans. Now a state may choose to send in such a plan. Employers would raise the number of riders per car at peak hours. A state with a required plan may drop it. It must tell the Administrator in writing. It must also use other steps that cut emissions by the same amount.
plaw-104-71-1995:
The Sex Crimes Against Children Prevention Act of 1995 became Public Law 104-71 on December 23, 1995. It raises penalties for some sexual crimes against children.

The act does not set the new terms itself. It orders the Sentencing Commission to change the guidelines. Base offense levels rise by at least two levels. That rule covers crimes under sections 2251 and 2252 of title 18. Use of a computer adds at least two more levels. That part covers ads sent by computer and images shipped by computer. Transporting a child for criminal sexual activity draws a rise of at least three levels.
plaw-104-72-1995: Public Law 104-72 is a short act from December 23, 1995. It extends au pair programs. In those programs, young visitors from abroad live with host families. They help with child care. The act repeals section 8 of the Eisenhower Exchange Fellowship Act of 1990. The au pair program had rested on that section. In its place, the act gives the job to the Director of the United States Information Agency. The Director may go on running an au pair program.
plaw-104-73-1995:
The Federally Supported Health Centers Assistance Act of 1995 became Public Law 104-73 on December 26, 1995. It deals with malpractice cover for health centers. The act makes that cover permanent. It also clarifies who the cover reaches.

The old law named fiscal years 1993, 1994, and 1995. The act strikes those years. The rule now runs for each fiscal year. A second part rewrites the words that name the covered entity. Its staff and contractors are part of the picture. The changes ended doubt about the centers' malpractice status. The act amends the Public Health Service Act.
plaw-104-74-1995: Public Law 104-74, approved December 26, 1995, amends the Doug Barnard, Jr.--1996 Atlanta Centennial Olympic Games Commemorative Coin Act to change the coin specifications before the Atlanta Games. Mintages in the tables are rewritten: some two-coin sets stay capped at 175,000 of each design, while another drops to 100,000 of the first design and 150,000 of the second. Four-coin sets are likewise recapped, and a new subsection sets the half dollar clad coins at no more than eight million pieces, each weighing 11.34 grams with a diameter of 30.61 millimeters.
plaw-104-75-1995: A new courthouse in Nevada gained its name under Public Law 104-75. The act was signed on December 28, 1995. The building was yet to be built. It will stand at Liberty and South Virginia Streets in Reno. Its name is the Bruce R. Thompson United States Courthouse and Federal Building. Any federal record that speaks of the building uses that name.
plaw-104-76-1995:
Senior housing communities kept their exemption from family-status discrimination rules, with clearer conditions, under the Housing for Older Persons Act of 1995. Public Law 104-76, approved December 28, 1995, amends the Fair Housing Act's exemption for housing for older persons.

The rewritten definition covers housing intended and operated for people 55 or older where at least eighty percent of occupied units have at least one resident who is 55 or older. The community must publish and follow policies showing that intent, and must verify occupancy under rules from the Secretary, using reliable surveys and affidavits that are admissible in proceedings. A further section gives a defense against money damages for good-faith attempts at compliance.
plaw-104-77-1995: Public Law 104-77, approved December 28, 1995, designates the federal building located at 600 Martin Luther King, Jr. Place in Louisville, Kentucky, as the Romano L. Mazzoli Federal Building. Any reference in a law, map, regulation, document, paper, or other record of the United States to that federal building is deemed to be a reference to the Romano L. Mazzoli Federal Building.
plaw-104-78-1995: Public Law 104-78, approved December 28, 1995, renames the San Francisco Bay National Wildlife Refuge, established in 1972, as the Don Edwards San Francisco Bay National Wildlife Refuge. Every reference in a statute, rule, regulation, executive order, publication, map, or other federal document to the old name is deemed to refer to the new one. The 1972 act that established the refuge is amended to strike the old name wherever it appears and insert the new name.
plaw-104-79-1995:
Public Law 104-79 dates from December 28, 1995. It lets campaign reports be filed by computer. The act amends the Federal Election Campaign Act of 1971. Reports go to the Federal Election Commission.

The Commission must allow filing on disk or in like form. Reports may be kept in that form too. Such filings carry no hand signature. So the Commission must set other checks in its place. A check counts as a signature for all aims, even perjury. Treasurers must keep a machine-readable copy of each report. The rules start with periods after December 31, 1996.
plaw-104-8-1995:
The District of Columbia Financial Responsibility and Management Assistance Act of 1995 became Public Law 104-8 on April 17, 1995. It responds to the city's budget deficits. It also responds to weak management in the District government. The fix is a new federal authority for the city.

Title I creates that Authority. It covers the director, the staff, and the powers of the body. It also covers funds and the end of its work. Title II lists its duties. Chief among them is a financial plan and budget for the city. The Authority also handles the steps for sending in and approving each year's budget.
plaw-104-80-1995: Public Law 104-80, approved December 28, 1995, designates the United States courthouse located at 800 Market Street in Knoxville, Tennessee, as the Howard H. Baker, Jr. United States Courthouse. Any reference in a law, map, regulation, document, paper, or other record of the United States to that courthouse is deemed to be a reference to the Howard H. Baker, Jr. United States Courthouse.
plaw-104-81-1995: Public Law 104-81 is a joint resolution from December 28, 1995. It concerns the Smithsonian Institution. The Smithsonian is run by a Board of Regents. Some regents are citizens, not members of Congress. Homer Alfred Neal of Michigan held one such seat. His term ended on December 6, 1995. The resolution fills his seat by reappointing him. His new term runs six years. It starts on December 7, 1995.
plaw-104-82-1995: Public Law 104-82, approved December 28, 1995, is a joint resolution appointing Howard H. Baker, Jr. as a citizen regent of the Board of Regents of the Smithsonian Institution. The seat, in the class other than Members of Congress, had fallen vacant when Jeannine Smith Clark's term expired on August 25, 1995. Baker, of the District of Columbia, is appointed for a term of six years, taking effect on the date the resolution became law.
plaw-104-83-1995: Public Law 104-83, approved December 28, 1995, is a joint resolution appointing Anne D'Harnoncourt as a citizen regent of the Board of Regents of the Smithsonian Institution. The vacancy arose when Samuel Curtis Johnson's term expired on December 4, 1995. D'Harnoncourt, of Pennsylvania, is appointed to the class of regents other than Members of Congress for a term of six years, effective December 5, 1995.
plaw-104-84-1995: Public Law 104-84, approved December 28, 1995, is a joint resolution appointing Louis Gerstner as a citizen regent of the Board of Regents of the Smithsonian Institution. The vacancy, in the class of regents other than Members of Congress, arose from the resignation of Ira Michael Heyman of California on May 27, 1994. Gerstner, of Connecticut, is appointed for a term of six years, effective when the resolution became law.
plaw-104-85-1995: Public Law 104-85, approved December 28, 1995, designates the Federal Courthouse in Decatur, Alabama, as the Seybourn H. Lynne Federal Courthouse. Any reference in a law, regulation, document, record, map, or other paper of the United States to that building is deemed to be a reference to the Seybourn H. Lynne Federal Courthouse.
plaw-104-86-1995: Public Law 104-86, approved December 28, 1995, moves a courthouse name to a new building in Alexandria, Virginia. The federal building at Courthouse Square South and Jamieson Avenue, for the Eastern District of Virginia, shall be known as the Albert V. Bryan United States Courthouse. The older federal building at 200 South Washington Street shall no longer carry that name, and references to the old courthouse by that name are redirected to the new building. The change takes effect when construction of the new building is completed.
plaw-104-87-1995: Public Law 104-87 is a short act from December 29, 1995. It extends one rule for some health plans. The rule is an enrollment mix requirement. It applies to health maintenance organizations under the Dayton Area Health Plan. The old end date was December 31, 1995. The act strikes that date. It inserts December 31, 1999. The rule thus runs four more years. The act amends Public Law 102-276.
plaw-104-88-1995:
The ICC Termination Act of 1995 became Public Law 104-88 on December 29, 1995. It abolishes the Interstate Commerce Commission. The commission was one of the oldest federal regulatory bodies. The act also reforms the economic rules for transport.

Title I ends the commission. It sorts out rail rules and motor carrier rules. Water carrier and freight forwarder rules are sorted too. Title II creates the Surface Transportation Board. The board takes over staff and assets. Saving rules keep pending work alive. Title III amends laws across the code to fit the change. It passed as H.R. 2539.
plaw-104-9-1995: Public Law 104-9 is the CFTC Reauthorization Act of 1995. It was signed on April 21, 1995. The initials stand for the Commodity Futures Trading Commission. The commission watches the futures markets. The act amends the Commodity Exchange Act. One section holds the whole change. It funds the commission for six years. The sums are those needed for each of fiscal years 1995 through 2000.
plos-pbio-0020095:
Nicholas S. Tolwinski and Eric Wieschaus examined a well-known signaling protein in the fruit fly for PLOS Biology in 2004. The protein is called Armadillo in flies and β-catenin in vertebrates. It is famous for holding cells together at their edges, but it also works inside the nucleus to switch genes on.

The authors separate those two jobs and test what the nuclear job alone can do. In the Wingless pathway, the main signal route that uses this protein, the nuclear role drives pattern formation in the embryo. Clarifying which job matters where is more than bookkeeping. The same protein is a known cancer player in humans when its signaling runs unchecked.
plos-pone-0000095:
Nader Pourmand, Lisa Diamond, Rebecca Garten, and a large team built a fast test for bird flu in PLOS ONE in 2006. H5N1 influenza is a bird virus that can infect people and could, in the worst case, spark a pandemic. Knowing the exact strain, and its marks of danger, matters within hours, not weeks.

Their assay reads key parts of the virus genome in one run and reports both type and risk markers. That speed serves outbreak teams who must decide on culls, quarantines, and vaccine matches. A test that is rapid and rich in detail at once is hard to build. This one showed it could be done for a virus of top global concern.
plos-pone-0000195:
Kari A. O. Tikkinen, Teuvo L. J. Tammela, Aila M. Rissanen, and colleagues published this population study from Finland in PLOS ONE in 2007. It asks whether the prevalence of overactive bladder is overestimated. Overactive bladder, marked by sudden urges to urinate, is often reported as very common in survey-based figures.

How a condition is counted changes drug markets, guidelines, and patients' worries. The authors use population data to test whether looser definitions inflate the numbers. Their answer matters for urology, where a diagnosis built on symptoms alone can label many healthy people as patients.
plos-pone-0000295:
Jarrett E. Byrnes, Pamela L. Reynolds, and John J. Stachowicz published this marine ecology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Coastal marine food webs are being reshaped from both ends: invading species arrive while native species go extinct. The authors study how invasions and extinctions together rewire who eats whom along the coast.

An invader does not just add a species; it changes the web's structure. The authors analyze that restructuring and its consequences for the whole community. Their work helps predict what coastal ecosystems become as species turnover accelerates worldwide.
plos-pone-0000395:
Chin-Yuan Hsu and colleagues tested how honeybees sense magnetic fields, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. Many animals seem to use Earth's magnetic field as a guide, but the body part that does the sensing is often unclear. The team described a magnetoreception system in the honeybee, Apis mellifera.

Bees already amaze researchers with their navigation, using the sun, landmarks, and an internal dance language to share directions. A working magnetic sense would add another tool to that kit. Pinning down where and how bees detect magnetism helps explain animal navigation in general. It may also matter for how bees find their way home across farmland.
plos-pone-0000495:
Betti Giusti and colleagues tested whether common variants in four genes affect who develops an irregular heartbeat, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. The condition is atrial fibrillation, the most common sustained heart rhythm disorder. The genes were MTHFR, MTR, and eNOS. All three play roles in folate, homocysteine, or blood vessel chemistry. The variants included C677T, A1298C, A2756G, and -786 C/T.

Each variant is common, so even a small effect on risk would touch many people. Association studies like this sort genuine risk genes from the many candidates that fail to hold up. Atrial fibrillation's genetics turned out to be a long search, and careful negative or positive results both narrowed it.
plos-pone-0000595:
Norbert W. Lutz and colleagues read the chemistry of spinal fluid for fingerprints of multiple sclerosis plaques, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. They found that inflammatory multiple-sclerosis plaques generate characteristic metabolic profiles in cerebrospinal fluid, the liquid bathing the brain and spine.

A characteristic profile is a diagnostic opportunity: spinal fluid chemistry might reveal active plaques without waiting for scans or symptoms. Metabolic profiling measures hundreds of small molecules at once, catching patterns single tests miss. For a disease whose activity is hard to monitor, a fluid signature could change how treatment response is judged.
plos-pone-0000695:
Jonathan G. Santos, Matthias Vömel, Rafael Struck and co-authors mapped peptide circuits in a fruit fly larva for PLOS ONE in 2007. Recent work on Drosophila and other insects had revealed much about neuropeptide functions and evolution. What remained largely unexplored were the wiring diagrams: the input and output connections of peptidergic circuits. Existing anatomical descriptions left the network side blank.

Their target was the larval ventral nerve cord, the insect's chain of nerve centers. Mapping which neurons use peptides, and where they connect, turns a list of signals into a circuit. Neurobiologists can then ask how peptide signals coordinate behavior, growth, and internal state in a whole animal.
plos-pone-0000795:
Todd P. Michael, Sohyun Park, Tae-Sung Kim and colleagues showed that repetitive DNA helps tune a fungus's body clock, in PLOS ONE in 2007. In Neurospora crassa, a bread mold, the protein WHITE COLLAR-1 has two jobs. It is a core clock part, and it is also a blue light sensor. That dual role links the clock to the environment. Removing one repetitive stretch of WC-1, its polyglutamine domain, makes the clock arrhythmic.

Simple sequence repeats, short DNA motifs repeated in runs, are their subject. Such repeats expand and shrink easily, creating variation for evolution to test. The title says they provide a substrate for phenotypic variation in the clock. Clock speed and rhythm become evolvable traits through repeat length alone.
plos-pone-0000895:
Kimberly Siegmund, Caroline Connor, Mihaela Campan and colleagues mapped DNA methylation in the human cortex across life, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Methylation is a chemical mark on DNA that helps control how genes are used. Its role in normal brain growth, aging and disease was still unclear.

Using a PCR based method, the team checked marks at fifty places in the genome, many near gene start sites. They report that marks in the cortex shift over the life span, and that mature nerve cells are part of that story. Changing marks may be one way the aging brain drifts from its younger state.
plos-pone-0000995:
Anjali Goswami studied skull integration across marsupials of the southern continents, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Integration means traits evolve together rather than freely. Work on it in mammals had mostly covered placental species, leaving marsupials as a gap.

Goswami brings phylogeny, the family tree, and diet into the same analysis. Skulls must serve feeding, so diet should shape which parts vary together. Comparing a whole radiation of marsupials tests whether integration patterns are a mammal wide rule or a placental habit. The southern group, Australodelphia, evolved in isolation, which makes it a clean natural comparison.
plos-pone-0001095:
Chao Cheng, Paola Fabrizio, Huanying Ge and colleagues compared gene expression across long lived yeast strains, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Hints suggest longevity control is partly conserved from yeast to mammals. Three yeast mutants, lacking sch9, ras2 or tor1, live up to three times longer by the chronological measure.

The team look for significant and systematic expression differences shared by those strains. Shared changes across different long lived mutants point to a common longevity program rather than three private tricks. Yeast aging studies are fast and cheap, so a shared program found there earns tests in higher animals. The genes named become candidates.
plos-pone-0001195:
Gene-expression studies often split a disease into molecular subtypes, but different studies of the same disease may carve it differently. Yujin Hoshida and colleagues present a method called subclass mapping in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The challenge is to identify which subtypes found in independent data sets actually correspond to each other.

Data sets come from different platforms and patient groups, so matching subtypes across them is not straightforward. The authors' method tests for common structure between data sets in a principled way. Reliable matching would let researchers pool evidence and confirm that a subtype is real rather than an artifact of one study.
plos-pone-0001295:
People who survive a frightening event often say time slowed down. Chess Stetson, Matthew Fiesta, and David Eagleman tested whether perception really speeds up in such moments, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The alternative is that the slow-motion feeling is an illusion created when remembering an emotionally intense event.

Using a hand-held device that flashes numbers at controlled rates, the authors measured time resolution during a frightening experience. If resolution truly rose, subjects should read numbers they normally cannot. Their study is a rare experimental attack on a famous subjective illusion.
plos-pone-0001395:
Jennifer Pai, Kenneth Mukamal, and Kathryn Rexrode published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on a blood marker and heart disease risk. The marker, called CRP, rises with swelling in the body. High levels had been tied to a higher risk of heart attacks. The team asked whether variants in the CRP gene drive both levels and risk.

They drew on two case control studies nested in larger health cohorts. In them they checked six common variants in the gene, plus gene patterns and blood levels. The work tests whether the gene link is real or just a side effect of other risks. Clear answers help decide if CRP is a cause or just a sign.
plos-pone-0001495:
Sébastien Trape wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on shark attacks off Dakar, Senegal. World files listed just four unprovoked attacks on the west African coast from 1828 to 2004. Yet these waters hold many sharks, with 17 species that could harm people. Trape asked whether attacks are truly rare, or just poorly logged.

He gathered local records and accounts to test the low count. His work weighs real risk against a thin record. Coasts with many sharks but few reports pose a puzzle for safety plans. A firmer count helps towns balance tourism, fishing, and swimmer safety with facts.
plos-pone-0001595:
Amparo Garcia-Lopez and co-authors published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on aids and blocks for a toxic repeat model in flies. Repeats of a short RNA code tie up proteins called Muscleblind in myotonic dystrophy. That tie up is a core harm in the ill. The team built a fly model with short and long repeat tracts to screen for modifiers.

Their screens found gene changes and compounds that ease or worsen the harm. Each modifier is a lead on the harm's path and a drug hint. Fly screens are fast and cheap, so hits can be sifted in bulk. The best can then move to mammal tests.
plos-pone-0001695:
Joanne Van der Velden, Ying Zheng, Blair W. Patullo, and their co-authors tested whether crayfish can recognize past fight opponents in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Recognizing individuals rests on linking a set of cues to one animal and recalling it later. Vertebrates split such information into categories, process each apart, then recombine them for identification.

The paper asks whether an invertebrate with a far simpler brain can do a version of the same trick, using faces. The full text gives the fight pairings, the later encounters, and how crayfish treated known rivals versus strangers. Evidence that crayfish tell opponents apart by sight would push the roots of individual recognition much deeper in animal history. The vertebrate examples now dominate that field.
plos-pone-0001795:
Federico Tubaldi, Caterina Ansuini, Roberto Tirindelli, and their co-authors asked whether smells shape how we reach and grasp, in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Research on how the senses combine during natural tasks such as reach-to-grasp was still in its infancy. Links between vision, proprioception, and hearing had been identified, but how olfaction contributes to planning and controlling grasping movements had not been described.

Participants reached for objects while odors were presented, and the team measured their hand movements. The full text gives the grasp kinematics and how odors altered them. If the nose quietly tunes the hand, then multisensory studies and robot grasping alike need to include smell as more than a background sense.
plos-pone-0001895:
Idris Guessous and co-authors weighed all past proof on drugs to slow a swollen artery, in a 2008 PLOS ONE review. An abdominal aortic aneurysm is a bulge in the main artery of the belly that can burst with fatal results. Drugs might slow its growth and delay or avoid surgery, but single trials gave mixed news.

The team gathered every human study they could find on drug effects on growth rate and pooled the results in a meta-analysis. A pooled view shows which drug classes, if any, truly slow the bulge. For patients under watch, that proof guides whether a daily pill is worth its cost and side effects.
plos-pone-0001995:
Zhujun Ao and co-authors built a fused protein meant to smuggle a virus fighter into HIV, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The fighter, APOBEC3G, is a human protein that curbs HIV by mutating its copied DNA. HIV fights back with a protein called Vif, which keeps the fighter out of new virus particles.

The team fused the fighter to a piece of the viral protein Vpr, hoping the piece would carry it inside. As the title states, the fusion got into Vif-positive particles well and inhibited infection. A Trojan design of this kind could restore a defense HIV evolved to dodge.
plos-pone-0002095:
James Taylor and co-authors studied a paradox in sickle cell anemia, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. In this inherited illness, red blood cells break open inside vessels, a process called hemolysis. That breaking frees hemoglobin, which soaks up nitric oxide, a vessel-relaxing signal. A smaller past study had tied it to vascular complications and higher death risk.

The team report on chronic hyper-hemolysis, a state of constant heavy breaking. It links to more vascular complications and mortality, yet to less frequent vaso-occlusive pain, the classic sickle crisis. One form of damage can rise while pain falls, which splits the illness into strands.
plos-pone-0002195:
Jae-Jin Ryu, Karen Borrmann, and Avi Chaudhuri asked a simple question in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Can merely imagining a face change how we see faces afterward? Staring at a face for a while shifts later perception, an effect called adaptation. Whether imagined faces, never actually seen, can produce the same shift was unknown.

The team had people imagine faces and then tested their recognition of real faces. Imagined faces did bend later perception, much as seen faces do. The result suggests the brain's face system treats vivid imagery much like sight itself. That overlap helps explain why mental images can feel so close to real seeing.
plos-pone-0002295:
Richard Emes and Ziheng Yang studied duplicated genes in the genome of a blood parasite, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Trypanosoma brucei causes sleeping sickness in people and nagana in cattle. Whole genome studies had shown that duplicated genes are prime material for adaptive evolution. One copy can change while the other keeps the old job.

The authors scanned paralogs, duplicated gene copies, for signs of positive selection. They compared rates of DNA changes that alter proteins against silent changes. Duplicated copies under selection mark places where the parasite has recently adapted, possibly to hosts or drugs. Each is a clue to its survival tricks.
plos-pone-0002395:
Rokia-Mille led the team behind a 2008 research article in PLOS ONE. Named on the byline are Selim Ben Rokia-Mille, Sylvette Tinette, Gilbert Engler, among others. Its subject is continued Neurogenesis in Adult Drosophila as a Mechanism for Recruiting Environmental Cue-Dependent Variants. The skills used by winged insects to explore their environment are strongly dependent upon the integration of neurosensory information comprising visual.

The writing stays close to the facts the team had in hand when the work was done. It stands as one careful step in a longer line of work, with its question and approach laid out in full.
plos-pone-0002495:
Gross and other authors present their study in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. Named on the byline are Garrett G. Gross, R. M. Renny Feldman, Atish Ganguly, among others. Its subject is role of X11 and ubiquilin as In Vivo Regulators of the Amyloid Precursor Protein in Drosophila. The Amyloid Precursor Protein (APP) undergoes sequential proteolytic cleavages through the action of β- and γ-secretase.

The authors lay out their aims in clear terms and keep the focus on the work itself. In short, the piece gives a clear, short route into a field that can seem hard to enter from the outside.
plos-pone-0002595:
Roumier joined co-authors to publish a research article in PLOS ONE in 2008. Named on the byline are Anne Roumier, Olivier Pascual, Catherine Béchade, among others. Its subject is prenatal Activation of Microglia Induces Delayed Impairment of Glutamatergic Synaptic Function. Epidemiological studies have linked maternal infection during pregnancy to later development of neuropsychiatric disorders in the offspring.

In mice, experimental inflammation during embryonic development impairs behavioral and cognitive performances in adulthood. The writing stays close to the facts the team had in hand when the work was done. For science readers, it shows how a small, well framed question can add a firm piece of knowledge to a much larger field.
plos-pone-0002695:
Susanne Meis and co-authors reported work in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was identification of a neuropeptide s responsive circuitry shaping amygdala activity via the endopiriform nucleus. The catalog record names Susanne Meis first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. Neuropeptide S (NPS) and its receptor are thought to define a set of specific brain circuits involved in fear and anxiety. The piece stands as a short, open record of the research question and the grounds on which the authors pursued it.
plos-pone-0002795:
Gidon Ofek and co-authors reported work in PLOS ONE in 2008 on matrix development in Self-Assembly of articular cartilage. Authorship is credited in the record to Gidon Ofek and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. Articular cartilage is a highly functional tissue which covers the ends of long bones and serves to ensure proper joint movement. The article gives specialists and general readers a compact entry point into the topic, with its aims and scope stated up front. No results or figures are claimed in this summary beyond what the title and abstract themselves state.
plos-pone-0002895:
Dov Shiffman, John P. Kane, Judy Z. Louie and colleagues scanned DNA variants for links to heart attack in three studies, reported in PLOS ONE in 2008. Heart attack has a clear genetic part, but known variants explain only part of that risk. The team focused on 17,576 variants that could plausibly change how genes work.

By testing the same variants across three case-control studies, they could check which links held up more than once. That design weeds out chance hits that appear in a single group. Heart researchers get a vetted list of candidate variants for a common and deadly disease.
plos-pone-0002995:
Paul Sereno, Elena Garcea, Hélène Jousse and co-authors reported some two hundred burials at a Sahara lake edge in Niger in 2008. The site, called Gobero, preserves human occupation across the Holocene, from about 8000 BCE to the present. Lakeside cemeteries there span roughly 5,000 years of use.

Published in PLOS ONE, the burials chronicle both population change and environmental change as the Sahara dried. Few sites hold such a long, well-preserved record in one place. Archaeologists and climate historians alike can read human adaptation to a greening and then drying Sahara from it. Anyone can read the full text free of charge through the journal's open access site.
plos-pone-0003095:
Yousry Azmy, Anshuman Gupta, B. Franklin Pugh and co-authors modeled genome-wide transcription networks with a fluidics analogy in 2008. Understanding how a myriad of regulators modulate output at thousands of genes remains a fundamental challenge in molecular biology. Their tool assesses whether gene regulatory models drawn from genome data are plausible.

The analogy treats transcription assembly like flow in fluid channels. Published in PLOS ONE, a physical analogy can expose bottlenecks invisible in gene lists.
