Digital scheduling projects and territory apps show early promise, they note. The closing challenge is naming which structural conditions let networks truly mature.
pmc-13287095:
Erkil Onur Günüç and Mustafa Salman test two feed additives in fattening lambs in a 2026 animal study. High-concentrate diets push fast growth but sour the rumen and waste nutrients. Twenty-eight weaned Bafra lambs were split into four groups: plain feed, chromium picolinate, sodium bicarbonate buffer, or both. They were fed individually for 63 days after a settling period, with growth, rumen fluid, digestibility, and carcass traits recorded.

Neither body weight nor intake differed by group, yet daily gain and feed efficiency answered to treatment in particular windows. The combined group gained and converted best between days 14 and 28 of the trial. Chromium alone cut rumen ammonia, raised protozoa counts, and improved fiber digestion, while the buffer's effects stayed limited. Carcass traits ignored all treatments, so the authors pitch the pairing for the adaptation phase of intensive feeding.
pmc-13288695:
Paula Christen and a long author list reflect on a 2026 account of a five-day hackathon meant to connect researchers, officials, and practitioners in Kenya. The January 2025 event in Nairobi, run by a London research center with the University of Nairobi, set challenges named by the health ministry and the veterinary directorate.

Six mixed teams of researchers, software engineers, and policymakers built prototype tools for outbreak surveillance, vaccine deployment, data quality checks, and health workforce estimates. Organizers describe the format as deliberate knowledge translation: short, structured teamwork that forces each side to use the others' skills. Their lessons argue that hackathons can speed research into practice and seed durable working relationships.
pmc-13289895:
Gerald Agyapong-Opoku and coauthors set out a 2026 scoping review protocol on non-drug help for anxiety and depression in youth aged 10 to 24. Both conditions rank among the top causes of disability in this age group and can shadow schooling and adult life. Programs vary hugely in form, place, and audience, so a systematic map is needed before stronger synthesis.

Six databases will be searched under institute guidance for scoping reviews, with reporting by a standard checklist. Any empirical work on interventions cutting anxiety or depression symptoms in the age band qualifies for charting. Two reviewers will select and chart studies on their own. Summaries will show the most common approaches and delivery modes.
pmc-13290195:
Some prenatal screening failures blamed on low fetal DNA may actually reflect Y chromosome problems in the fetus, Siqi Hu and colleagues reported in 2026. The retrospective study covers 24,101 pregnant women who had noninvasive prenatal testing between January 2023 and January 2025.

Sex chromosome abnormalities were far more common in the low fetal fraction group than in the adequate group, an increase the authors put at roughly 78-fold. All eight abnormal cases in the low group involved the Y chromosome, which the standard method uses to estimate fetal fraction. Re-estimating with a different method, FF-QuantSC, lifted every case to a reportable level and let the test flag the abnormalities. Hu and colleagues advise re-checking before declaring a test failed.
pmc-13290895:
Bypass veins rescue blood flow where the iliac vein is squeezed, Ke Hu and colleagues show in a simulation study from 2026. In iliac vein compression syndrome an artery pinches the vein against the spine, and collateral channels sometimes grow around the blockage; the team modeled what those channels do to flow.

Two patient-specific 3D models, one with well-developed collaterals and one without, were built from CT angiography and run under body-like flow conditions. Without collaterals the model showed sprawling reflux and vortices, a peak pressure gap of 20,190 Pa, and wall shear stress up to 56 Pa. With collaterals, pressure gap fell to 619 Pa, shear to 10 Pa, and outflow to the vena cava rose about 39%. Hu and colleagues read collaterals as a real compensatory mechanism, while cautioning the work is mechanistic, not clinical proof.
pmc-13290995:
Young adults in active cancer care are the focus of a 2026 pragmatic trial led by Eran Ben-Arye on integrative oncology, where supportive methods sit alongside standard treatment. Patients aged 18 to 45 were offered a personal consultation plus six weekly sessions aimed at quality-of-life concerns.

Of 180 patients, 137 attended at least four sessions and counted as highly adherent, while the rest formed a low-adherence comparison shaped by patient choice. At six weeks the high-adherence group reported larger gains on symptom and wellbeing scales, with clearer gains again in patients aged 40 to 45 than in younger peers. Fatigue, anxiety, and breathing scores moved most in that older subgroup, which hints that benefit may depend on age as well as attendance.
pmc-13291295:
Burning one tumor can shift immunity in a far tumor. Kun Zhao leads a 2026 mouse study of heat ablation. Past work looked mostly at leftover tumor near the burn. Distant tumors may gain or lose immune support too.

Mice bore tumors on both body sides. One side got full or partial heat ablation. The far side served as the test site. Killer immune cells rose there at first. By day nine, the mood turned suppressive. One immune brake, CTLA-4, rose at that point. Adding a drug against that brake helped. Far tumors grew slower and held more killer cells.
pmc-13291895:
Lars Breum Christiansen and co-authors evaluate a 2026 preschool program, Ball-based Play in Preschool, designed to weave ball games into daily routines. Eight preschools took part in a non-randomized wait-list design, and parents answered questionnaires about their children's play. The team built a Ball Play Index combining how often children play, how much they enjoy it, and their skill level.

Baseline answers from 429 families varied widely: ball sports participation ran from 14 to 30 percent across settings, and any-sport participation from 31 to 80 percent of children surveyed. Gender, disability status, and parental background all tracked with the outcomes. In the impact group of 108 children, the program showed no significant effect on either the index or leisure ball sports participation. The authors advise future programs to weigh club capacity and starting activity levels.
pmc-13292995:
Serrena Singh and colleagues compare, in a 2026 study, two related growth switches, YAP and TAZ, that drive cell growth in the liver. Though close cousins, they may act very differently, so the team grew liver clones dominated by each one.

YAP clones quickly turned stem-like, drew in inflammatory immune cells, and were then cleared. TAZ clones instead calmed inflammation, lasted, and drove huge organ growth with more deaths. Blocking the immune cells let YAP clones grow freely. In patient data, bowel cancers high in YAP had better five-year survival than those high in TAZ. The two switches thus act as distinct disease drivers.
pmc-13293695:
Emma K. Ward, Nick Simpson, and Clare Press test, in a 2026 study, how breaking a learned pattern in the environment affects spotting new events. Perception leans on expectation, yet how the brain updates when patterns shift is still debated.

Six experiments had people detect visual targets around and inside a circle where outer items followed a place or angle rule that then changed without warning. Detection fell for all events right after a rule break, based on modeling the authors report. Recovery took several trials after a rare break but became instant when breaks came often. Expectation thus aids seeing broadly, at a cost when rules change.
pmc-13293795:
Lidan Zhang and co-authors pool, in a 2026 review, infection risk for the gut drug vedolizumab in inflammatory bowel disease, comparing it with rival drug classes and placebo. Infection safety shapes drug choice in lifelong gut illness, and pooled rates vary widely by study.

Sixty-six studies with 24,000 patients were combined, with infection grading set to a shared standard. Overall infection incidence pooled at 13.08% in the authors' model, led by airway infections, while serious infections stayed rare. Risk matched tumor necrosis factor drugs and placebo, but ran higher than with ustekinumab. Wide spread between studies limits the pooled rate's use.
pmc-13293995:
Ying Li, Yanxia Cai, and Xiaoyan Xu report a 2026 case where many skin nodules were the first sign of angioimmunoblastic T-cell lymphoma. Skin involvement in that lymphoma usually means rash or itching, so firm nodules mislead easily. Their patient was a 53-year-old man with a 1-month history of painless lumps on trunk and upper limbs, sized 0.5–2 cm, plus dark red plaques.

Tests showed mild anemia, raised inflammation markers, low IgA, high IgE, and widespread lymph node swelling. Biopsy showed lost node structure with atypical cells positive for CD3, CD4, PD-1, and EBER, giving stage III disease. Six cycles of chidamide plus CHOP brought full remission, still holding at 6 months.
pmc-13294295:
Sinja Kristiansen and coauthors census gonorrhea care at six Swedish university clinics in a 2026 study. Cases from 2022 totaled 1,060, about a third of all national cases that year, with 27.3% women, 72.4% men, and 4 transgender persons in the reported breakdown. Nucleic acid tests covered urine, genital, and rectal sampling sites, and drug resistance was charted.

Positivity ran highest in genital samples from women and in rectal samples, mostly among men who have sex with men. Resistance hit 43.7% for ciprofloxacin and 9.4% for azithromycin in the reported shares. Multi-site infection and fading drug options make management complex, the authors conclude.
pmc-13294395:
Mengqi Yang and a large team review multifunctional nano-drugs for solid tumors in a 2026 article organized by tumor neighborhood type. Potency alone fails when vessels block entry, stroma blocks spread, and immunity stays off. Platforms now bundle longer circulation, vessel and stroma tuning, trigger-based release, immune priming, and imaging guidance in one particle.

Human leakiness effects vary, targeting gains in people stay uncertain, and each added module complicates manufacturing and safety proof. The authors sort designs by barrier, goal, readout, and evidence strength. Future wins likely come from matching simpler platforms to measured tumor types, not from piling on features.
pmc-13294495:
Gabriela Gavalova and colleagues probe emotion reading errors in psychotic disorders with aggression history in a 2026 study. Groups held 79 people with psychosis plus past interpersonal aggression, 72 with psychosis alone, and 86 healthy controls. A lifelike task showed faces, voices, and both together across 12 emotions, scoring accuracy and confusion patterns by valence and arousal.

Accuracy stepped down cleanly across groups, worst in the aggression group. That group also more often mistook negative feelings for positive ones. Thinking speed and emotion word knowledge predicted scores most strongly, with schooling, gender, and past substance history adding smaller effects. Group status still mattered after all adjustments.
pmc-13294695:
Alişan Burak Yaşar and Anıl Gündüz propose a new psychotherapy framework called Smart Therapy in a 2026 article. Many proven treatment manuals exist, yet dropout and resistance stay common and clinicians often mix methods without shared rules. No standard guidance tells clinicians how to choose and order interventions for each person.

Assessment comes first across three domains: bodily prerequisites, deep memory patterns from hardship, and unhelpful thinking habits. Treatment then follows five sequenced levels, starting with shared goals and health screening before matched psychological work. The model aims to close the gap between research protocols and everyday practice by tying each intervention choice to assessed need.
pmc-13296195:
Anakha Udayakumar and co-authors test, in 2026, whether a chemical change on the protein OSTM1 explains how the kinase LRRK1 drives bone-eating cells. Mice lacking LRRK1 develop overly dense bone because their osteoclasts cannot break bone down, and tagging of OSTM1 fades in those cells.

A version of OSTM1 that mimics the tag partly restored bone breakdown in deficient cells, while a version blocking the tag did not. Mice built with the mimicking variant grew normally, and adding it to deficient mice boosted osteoclast activity and bone formation. The authors name OSTM1 tagging as a key link worth targeting.
pmc-13297695:
Ontario-wide records show CAR T-cell therapy for lymphoma performs in everyday care much as it did in trials, according to a 2026 population study led by Lee Mozessohn. Using provincial administrative databases, the team followed patients with diffuse large B-cell lymphoma treated after relapse or failed earlier therapy.

Survival and toxicity in routine practice matched the pivotal trial results, and hospital use resembled figures from other registry reports. The authors describe the treatment as relatively safe in real-world hands for this aggressive lymphoma. They also argue that future studies should build in formal health technology assessment, so decision makers can weigh clinical gains against the therapy's considerable demands on the system.
pmc-13297795:
Clear aligners made in the dental office move front teeth sideways accurately but rotate them less faithfully, found a 2026 retrospective analysis by Gina Marie Georgi and colleagues. They compared planned and achieved positions in 21 dental arches from 14 patients treated with in-office SureSmile aligners.

Side-to-side shifts missed the plan by small margins, all under the 0.5 mm clinical threshold, with vertical movement off by 0.38 mm on average. Angular control was weaker: angulation differed by 3.42 degrees and axial rotation by 4.50 degrees, both beyond the 2-degree threshold. The authors suggest clinicians plan extra correction for rotations and counsel patients accordingly.
pmc-13298595:
A clotting protein outperformed the usual blood markers for spotting appendicitis in children, report Hilmi Onur Kabukçu and co-authors in a 2026 single-center study. They compared 145 children who had CT scans for abdominal pain: 62 with nonspecific pain, 44 with uncomplicated appendicitis, and 39 with complicated disease.

Fibrinogen rose stepwise across the three groups and separated appendicitis from nonspecific pain with an AUC of 0.95, ahead of CRP, white cell counts, and related ratios. It also held up as an independent predictor in adjusted analysis. The authors propose fibrinogen as a promising addition to workups, pending larger prospective confirmation.
pmc-13298995:
Math can guide the design of virus cocktails that hunt drug-resistant bacteria, argue Rob J de Boer and colleagues in a 2026 modeling paper. They extended a mouse-calibrated model to human phage therapy, where several bacterial strains and several phages interact and resistance keeps evolving.

Fitting the model to one successful human case, they found success hinged on how resistant the bacteria already were before treatment and on giving diverse cocktails early. Once a good cocktail was in place, fine-tuning infection rates mattered little. Resistant strains surged as sensitive ones fell. Their prescription: hit hard and early with a varied set of phages to raise the barrier against resistance.
pmc-13300095:
The Asian corn borer damages maize across much of Asia, and its immune defenses shape how well microbial pest control works. Xinran Jia and colleagues report a 2026 functional study of OfPGRP-B, a peptidoglycan recognition protein in this moth. They produced the protein in Escherichia coli and ran a battery of laboratory assays.

OfPGRP-B killed bacteria only weakly, yet it clumped them strongly and cut peptidoglycan with amidase activity. It also boosted activation of the prophenoloxidase cascade when bacterial wall material was present, without changing melanization. The authors read the protein as a working part of borer immunity, useful knowledge for designing biological controls that target host defenses.
pmc-13300995:
Two back-wall nerve blocks spared opioids after gallbladder keyhole surgery in a 2026 randomized trial by Özlem Turhan and colleagues. One hundred twenty adults were split three ways: erector spinae plane block, thoracic paravertebral block, or intravenous pain relief alone. Everyone received standard anesthesia plus paracetamol, tenoxicam, and patient-controlled tramadol for comparison.

Over the first day, the intravenous group used 135.78 milligrams of tramadol, against 101.05 with the erector spinae block and 95.67 with the paravertebral block. Pain scores and rescue needs also favored both blocks, and recovery quality scores rose. The erector spinae block was quicker to perform, with no complications in any arm.
pmc-13303495:
Rawan AlSaad and co-authors present a 2026 systematic review of artificial intelligence tools that predict heavy bleeding after childbirth. Standard risk scores rely on fixed factors and can miss changes that unfold during labor.

Following PRISMA guidance, the team reviewed studies from 2015 to 2025 and included 33 papers. Most work appeared after 2023, used past records from a single site, and aimed to sort risk before delivery. Classic machine learning dominated, all datasets were closed, and outside validation was rare. Shared labeling rules, larger shared datasets, and testing during real care are presented as next steps.
pmc-13303595:
Karuna Rasineni and Patricia Sue Grigson write a 2026 editorial introducing a collection on GLP-1 receptor agonist drugs. These long-acting medicines have changed care for obesity and type 2 diabetes, conditions that carry a heavy global toll.

Papers in the collection weigh benefits, harms, and costs across drug versions. Other papers look at effects after weight-loss surgery and on the brain reward system, eyes, heart, liver, and swollen limbs after breast cancer care. Other papers pool trial data and adverse event reports to measure gut and other side effects. The set frames both promise and caution for wider use.
pmc-13303695:
Carlotta Franceschi and co-authors review biologic injections for kneecap joint problems in a 2026 systematic synthesis. Such products are well studied for whole-knee arthritis, but proof for wear limited to the joint behind the kneecap has stayed thin.

Four databases were searched for human studies of platelet-rich plasma or mesenchymal stromal cell products in kneecap cartilage damage or arthritis. Nine studies qualified, split between the two product types. Despite weak study quality overall, patients generally improved on clinical scores and sometimes on scans, and both approaches beat comparison care. Larger, stronger trials are still needed before routine use.
pmc-13304195:
Riya Rawal, Anita Thyagarajan, and Ravi P. Sahu study a smoke pollutant's effect on lung cancer cells in a 2026 laboratory report. Benzo[a]pyrene, found in tobacco smoke and cooked food, is a known carcinogen, but its sway over targeted drug response was unclear.

Cancer cells exposed to the pollutant did not die more, yet they moved more, grew more, formed more colonies, and shed more tiny particles. A cell receptor blocker and a fat-processing blocker stopped those changes, tying them to one signaling path. Reassuringly, the pollutant did not blunt the targeted drugs tested, and the receptor emerges as a possible new drug target.
pmc-13305595:
Vida Garousi, Fattaneh Khalaj, and Elham Mirzaian present a 2026 case of a primary neuroendocrine tumor in the testicle, a growth making up under one percent of testicle tumors. Vague signs and look-alike growths make this rare cancer easy to misread.

A 21-year-old man had a painless left testicle lump with rich blood flow and calcium flecks on scans, while blood tumor markers stayed normal. Removal showed a neat, slow-growing tumor with the classic speckled cell pattern, and stain tests confirmed hormone-type cells with very low growth activity. Under the 2022 World Health Organization scheme it classed as the prepubertal type, needing long follow-up.
pmc-13308595:
Ayuba Akinpelu and co-authors show in 2026 that long exposure to high fluid pressure dulls how moving cells read the physical world around them. Pressure kept cells less swayed by base stiffness, fluid thickness, flow force, and flow block for days after the cue was lifted.

The team traced the shift to a quieter Rho and MRTF path, with a backup sensing mode that needs no myosin pull to work. Stiff bases then sped the primed cells by firming their grip points and spreading them to the cell edge. Models foresaw the shift, and dish tests bore it out. Pressure may thus prime wandering cancer cells in lasting ways.
pmc-13309195:
Allison Crawford and Tristan Glatard urge in 2026 urgent steps for suicide prevention as young people turn to chat based AI tools in distress, often before family or doctors. In a United States poll of 1060 teens aged 13 to 17 years, 72 percent said they use an AI helper, and 52 percent do so often.

Most AI suicide tools lack sound guards, and some suits claim chat tools steered youth toward attempts, means, and farewell notes. The authors say tools must own their AI nature, explain their advice, prompt users to ask why, and act as a bridge to human care, never a wall. Human bonds stay the core shield, so tools should push people toward live support, not replace it.
pmc-13309395:
Giulia Giacomucci and colleagues report a 2026 study on blood tests that may warn of early Alzheimer changes. The patients had subjective cognitive decline, meaning they felt their memory slipping while standard tests stayed normal. The team asked which blood marker best tracks later thinking changes.

Seventy-six patients gave blood and took detailed thinking tests at the start and again two years later. A marker called p-tau217 tracked memory decline most closely, with mid-range results falling between clear negative and clear positive groups. Two other markers showed weaker or mixed links. The authors suggest p-tau217 may help spot who needs closer follow-up in this early stage.
pmc-13309895:
Anastasios Koulaouzidis writes a 2026 letter to the editor about ultrasound checks for a swallowed capsule before bowel camera exams. A patency capsule is first swallowed to prove the gut is open; finding where it sits matters before the camera capsule follows. A study by Matsuura and colleagues had praised ultrasound as a radiation-free first step.

The letter argues that scans where the capsule was not seen were counted as negative results, which inflates the claimed accuracy. Ultrasound located the capsule clearly in 28 of 34 patients, while 6 of 34 stayed unclear and still needed CT scanning in the cited study. A not-seen scan should count as undecided, the author holds. The piece urges honest reporting of test limits.
pmc-13310395:
Yaodie Peng and co-authors relate lung exercise capacity to airway and air-sac damage in COPD in a 2026 study. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease narrows airways and destroys air sacs in differing mixes per patient. Whether air-sac loss or airway thickening tracks exercise limits more closely was unclear.

Ninety-three stable patients underwent lung function tests, chest CT scans, and exercise testing. Scan measures split patients into four types: normal, air-sac dominant, airway dominant, and mixed. Air-sac dominant and mixed patients showed worse airflow ratios in the reported results. Statistical models tied each scan measure to exercise outcomes. The authors conclude air-sac damage tracks exercise capacity more strongly than airway thickness in this group.
pmc-13310495:
Chuan-Yen Sun and co-authors validate a simplified home sleep test against the lab standard in a 2026 study. Sleep apnea is common and needs early spotting, yet lab testing is heavy and home kits often need many sensors. A chest-worn heart monitor that reads breathing from heart-lung coupling could ease setup.

Adults suspected of apnea at three Taiwan medical centers wore the device during full lab sleep study nights. A total of 479 participants enrolled across the centers, and the device event index was compared with the lab apnea score for each night. The index correlated strongly with the lab score in the reported results. The authors present the single-sensor test as a practical screen.
pmc-13310695:
Jianbo Cheng led a 2026 mouse study on whether a milk protein food can help the gut heal after Salmonella infection. Older adult mice were given the germ that causes severe bowel injury, slow repair, and swelling. The team tested a casein based feed given before and during infection.

Mice on the feed survived better, showed less illness, and kept a healthier gut lining. The feed also shifted gut germs toward types that make lactate, which raised signals that help stem cells regrow tissue. Blocking those signals removed the benefit, which supports the proposed chain. Results suggest a food based route worth testing further for gut repair.
pmc-13310795:
Evans Nii Ayitey MacCready presents a 2026 case of brain abscess that revealed a hidden heart defect in a young adult. A man aged 18 years had a seizure after four days of frontal headache. Exam found clubbed fingers, excess blood signs, and a heart murmur, which hinted at a birth defect of the heart.

Brain scans showed a right frontal abscess, and heart tests found an unrepaired septal defect with a shared upper chamber. Mixed blood flow can let germs bypass lung filtering and reach the brain. Drainage surgery cleared the abscess fully, with stable health at six months. Heart checks matter when brain abscess has no clear source.
pmc-13311095:
Danling Hu and colleagues compare pain relief methods after stomach cancer surgery in a 2026 network study. Many nerve block and spine methods can ease pain and cut opioid use, and each may also shift immune balance. Past trials were pooled to rank eleven plans head to head.

Twenty three trials with 1,700 patients fed the network. Several regional methods beat plain systemic drugs on pain scores. One chest wall block ranked best for long term pain at rest and on movement. Spine based relief cut opioid use most and raised a helpful immune cell ratio. Proof quality ran low to moderate, so rankings need care.
pmc-13311195:
Andriana Koutsandrea and colleagues track antioxidant defenses in Baltic Sea zooplankton in a 2026 field study. Tiny drifting animals face warming, freshening, low oxygen, and algae blooms that raise cell stress. Whether their antioxidant shields flex enough to block damage across sites and seasons was tested.

Samples came from four northern Baltic sites in summer and autumn 2023. Two shield enzymes answered to distinct drivers, split by which animal types ruled each sample. One enzyme ran high in copepod rich groups, the other in water flea rich groups. Damage marks stayed low and steady throughout, which suggests flexible shields held cells safe.
pmc-13311295:
Raphael Moll and co-authors, in 2026, share a study of two-species biofilms built around the pathogen Stenotrophomonas maltophilia. Mixed biofilms resist drugs and keep infections going, so their layout over time matters.

The team grew the bacterium with Pseudomonas aeruginosa or Staphylococcus aureus and watched with light-sheet microscopy plus cell counting. The films formed clear top-to-bottom zones, and gene activity switched on and off in time-bound waves that differed by layer. Iron transport stood out in the contest for space. The partner species also dulled each other's signals, showing how neighbors reshape growth.
pmc-13311995:
Qiuyun Jiang and co-authors in 2026 present a study on microbe partnerships that burn methane without oxygen in deep-sea cold seep mud. This process trims how much methane, a strong greenhouse gas, escapes the sea floor.

Sediments from the South China Sea were incubated with labeled methane, tracers, and bacteria-blocking treatments. Distinct archaeal and bacterial groups shared the work under differing chemical conditions. When some partners were blocked, communities shifted to backup pathways and kept overall methane use steady. The overlap gives the system resilience, a point that matters for plans to curb methane release.
pmc-13312495:
Ming Liu and co-authors present a 2026 study of how the fungus Botrytis deweyae invades Polygonatum cyrtonema, a medicinal plant it blights with gray mold. The fungus was first described on daylilies and has lately turned up on new hosts, yet its infection playbook on this plant was unknown.

Microscopy at three scales showed two entry routes: direct penetration of the leaf surface, aided by gelatinous secretions and infection cushions, and entry through the leaf's stomata. Transcriptome analysis highlighted fat metabolism, oxidoreductase activity, and MAPK signaling as the machinery of attack. The host's high osmotic pressure appears to trip the fungal MAPK pathway, with the Hog1 component prominent, switching on antioxidant enzymes that let the fungus manage the stress. The authors offer the map as a basis for targeted gray mold control.
pmc-13312595:
Lorena Jiménez-Sánchez and colleagues examine, in a 2026 study, how the brain's face area develops alongside higher social regions in childhood. The fusiform face area answers to faces from early infancy. One idea holds that social brain regions, the medial prefrontal cortex and superior temporal sulcus, guide its tuning, while another credits an inborn template in the amygdala.

Using an open dataset of children aged 3 to 12 and adults watching a movie during brain scanning, the team measured how adult-like each child's responses were. Older children looked more mature in every region. Children whose right face area responded more maturely also showed stronger wiring between that area and the right prefrontal social region. Their superior temporal sulcus responses were more adult-like on both sides. The authors read the pattern as early evidence of co-development.
pmc-13313195:
Mohammed Khudair leads a scoping review, published in 2026, of what shapes vaccine choices among pregnant women in the UK. The team used the SAGE matrix on vaccine hesitancy and asked how views (intent) differ from real uptake, and how story-based and number-based studies differ.

Five databases were searched, and 49 primary studies from 2010 to 2025 were kept out of 2,326 records found. The review counted 222 factors from 32 studies that used interviews and 114 factors from 30 studies that used numbers, with some studies in both groups. Interview work stressed beliefs about safety and benefit and the weight of advice from health staff. Number-based work stressed age, ethnic group, and level of social and money hardship. The map helps clinics see which levers may raise uptake.
pmc-13314395:
Minseo Cho and colleagues test a freeze-dried rocket plant extract on eye cells in a 2026 study tied to diabetic eye disease and age-related macular degeneration. Both diseases harm the retinal pigment layer and involve lasting inflammation plus high levels of VEGF, a vessel growth signal.

The team used ARPE-19 cells, a human retinal cell line, and stressed them with a drug called thapsigargin. The extract caused no cell harm at any dose tried, by the tests reported. At a dose of 1 mg per mL, it cut VEGF gene activity by 32 percent and VEGF release by 34 percent as stated in the report. It also eased the calcium surge the stress drug caused. It also curbed the NF-kappaB inflammation switch named in the title. The finds hint the plant extract may guard the retina.
pmc-13314595:
Bing Chen and An-Yue Jin argue in a 2026 perspective that generative AI should serve meaning-centered care for older adults, not just symptom checks. AI tools are rushing into mental health work, but most uses rest on screening, sorting, and risk spotting.

For old people, mental health often turns on deeper questions: lost roles, a broken sense of self, loneliness, dignity, and legacy. The authors insist AI must not stand in for clinicians, nurses, social workers, or family carers. Instead they frame it as a shared stage for human care, in a model with four steps: sensing, narrating, connecting, and governing. In that model, AI spots cues of existential strain, backs life-review talks, helps build dignity-keeping stories, and links elders to human networks. The piece draws on dignity therapy, life review, and care ethics.
pmc-13314695:
Aykut Aykaç and colleagues test a slim-sheath twist on laser prostate surgery in a 2026 study. Holmium laser enucleation clears benign prostate growth at any size, but the wide scopes it uses can hurt the urethra.

Dedicated slim systems exist to cut that risk, yet many hospitals lack them. The team used a common 21 Fr internal urethrotomy sheath, with passive bladder drainage through a small suprapubic tube, then standard tissue grinding. They compared 47 patients on the new method with 48 on standard surgery, treated from January 2021 to May 2023, as counted in the report. Short-term function and safety were set side by side. If the slim route holds up, low-resource theaters can offer gentler prostate surgery with tools already on the shelf.
pmc-13314795:
Jose Almirall and Tatiana Trejos review forensic study of paint, tape, and glass for Interpol in a 2026 paper. The review gathers gains in methods for these three common trace materials since the 20th Interpol symposium in October 2022.

It spans journal papers, reports, and books, plus new standard guides such as ASTM methods, and shifts in how the materials are made and where. More than 45 journals and sources carried peer-reviewed work on the three evidence types over the past three years, by the count given in the report. Leading outlets named include the Journal of Forensic Sciences, Forensic Chemistry, and Forensic Science International. The digest helps crime labs match their practice to the newest proven methods.
pmc-13314995:
Xuexue Fu and colleagues add ginger to a Guizhou chili ferment and watch flavor change, in work published in 2026. Zao Chili takes long to ferment and its quality swings, so the team tested ginger as a steering aid.

Sequencing showed ginger shifted the microbe cast. Mid-ferment, two yeasts named Kazachstania and Hanseniaspora ruled the ginger batch with shares of 74.69 percent and 17.16 percent as given in the report, while other yeasts led the plain batch. Nitrite ran lower in the ginger batch by a margin of 30.24 percent on two check days, as stated. Scent scans on day 20 found far richer aroma output, partly from ginger terpenes, and esters rose too. The work ties ginger to safer, tastier ferments through microbe control.
pmc-13315995:
Paul J. Young offers a logical reading in 2026 of the data on best oxygen targets for unresponsive adults in intensive care after cardiac arrest. Interest grew after early studies linked high blood oxygen soon after resuscitation with more deaths and worse brain outcomes at discharge.

He stresses a key confounder. Patients in shock with poor circulation often get more inspired oxygen because pulse readings become unreliable when perfusion is weak, so high oxygen may mark sicker patients rather than cause harm. Sorting cause from marker is central before tight oxygen limits can be advised with confidence.
pmc-13316195:
Daniel Joelsons and a very large team report in 2026 the first Brazilian comparison of extracorporeal resuscitation against standard resuscitation for in-hospital cardiac arrest that does not respond to usual care. The extracorporeal method uses a machine to circulate and oxygenate blood while the heart is stopped.

Hospital survival was 43.7 percent with the extracorporeal program versus 13.6 percent with conventional care in the headline comparison. As the country's first such program, the cohort sets a local benchmark and shows what organized rapid deployment can achieve for refractory arrests in a large hospital.
pmc-13316295:
M Tawana and co-authors offer a 2026 review of plant-based ways to kill a major cattle tick in Africa, where heavy use of factory-made chemicals has bred resistant ticks. Their search, the first of its kind for the region, gathers tests of local plant extracts against this pest.

Following standard review rules, the team screened 2,046 records and kept 20 studies from 2000 to 2025 that fit strict rules. Extracts came from 26 plant families, led by the mint and daisy families. Among kept studies, 40 percent found high tick death rates, 35 percent found middling effects, and 25 percent found weak ones. Whole regions lack published tests, so the authors urge wider trials before farm-ready products can follow.
pmc-13316695:
Kiran Batool and co-authors made, in a 2026 study, edible active films from potato starch loaded with extract from potato peels, aimed at keeping fresh-cut potatoes from spoiling. Peel extract was pulled out with water and ultrasound, a green method, then blended into films at levels from 2 to 10 percent.

Higher extract levels gave smoother, thicker films that let less water vapor through and broke down fully in soil within about fifteen days for low mixes, unlike plastic controls. Germ-fighting and antioxidant strength rose with dose, and the strongest films visibly slowed browning and spoilage on cut potatoes. Strength dipped slightly at top doses, a trade-off makers can tune. Waste peels thus become packaging that protects their own crop.
pmc-13317195:
Xin Wen and co-authors show, in a 2026 study, that cassia seed extract fights hepatitis B virus in liver cells. They trace the effect of the traditional food-medicine herb to one compound, aloe emodin. The virus drives cirrhosis and liver cancer worldwide, with few good treatments.

The water extract cut viral copying in step with dose. Of several seed compounds tested, aloe emodin hit hardest. Both extract and compound switched on the interferon defense path and raised a guard gene called IFITM1; deleting that gene badly weakened the antiviral effect. The seed's benefit thus runs through the body's own alarm system, a fresh angle for chronic hepatitis B drug hunting.
pmc-13318395:
Jagdeep Sedha leads a 2026 diagnostic accuracy study of a deep neural network. The model spots atrial fibrillation and flutter in long-term heart rhythm recordings. Both conditions raise stroke risk yet often pass unnoticed. Training drew on public sets, earlier study data, and hospital recordings.

Testing used 1,039 recordings from 1,010 patients at Kuopio University Hospital. Experts had checked every recording. At the level of time segments, the model reached 96.4 percent sensitivity. Specificity stayed above 99.99 percent across the test set. Whole recordings were caught with full sensitivity, and false alarms stayed rare. Most false alarms involved other rhythm problems. Performance held across ages, illnesses, and poor-quality traces, suggesting less manual review work.
pmc-13318595:
Yanli Zhang and colleagues present a 2026 case report on treating a venous malformation beside the eye with bloodletting at the Taiyang acupoint, a traditional Chinese medicine method. Their patient was a 27-year-old woman whose right eye area swelled and turned greenish when she looked down, then settled when her head rose.

Ultrasound and CT confirmed the malformation, which measured 2.0×1.28 cm at diagnosis in the affected area. Weekly bloodletting removed about 2 mL per session, and after six months follow-up ultrasound showed the lesion smaller, with no growth seen. Detailed scans around single sessions suggested the method briefly reduces blood flow into the lesion, easing swelling and pressure, though the authors limit their claim to this one localised case.
pmc-13318795:
Alessia Mariacher leads a large team reporting, in 2026, an integrated watch system for a raccoon parasite in Italy. Raccoons are an invasive species carrying Baylisascaris procyonis, a worm dangerous to people and animals. The parasite first appeared in Arezzo province raccoons in 2021. The team combined carcass checks, lab tests, mapping, and public outreach.

From 2021 to 2024, they examined 102 raccoons. The parasite turned up in 34 animals, or 33.3 percent of those tested. No infection appeared in 169 possible intermediate hosts, 30 wolves, or 15 at-risk dog samples. All positive raccoons shared one genetic type, suggesting a single escape event. Mapping marked a high-risk core of 265 km2 for targeted action.
pmc-13318995:
Shi Feng and colleagues propose, in a 2026 review, a mitochondria-centred defence network that helps HPV-positive cervical cancer resist ferroptosis, an iron-driven cell death. Standard chemoradiation often fails against these tumours. The authors centre their framework on mitochondrial STAT3 and the enzyme DHODH. Both sit inside the cell's power plant.

Viral proteins E6 and E7 keep tumour cells under constant growth and oxidative pressure. That pressure raises dependence on mitochondrial control systems. Mitochondrial STAT3 may keep energy production efficient and limit electron leaks. DHODH may supply a protective antioxidant inside the membrane. Together they could hold back membrane damage and cell death. The review maps drug strategies against this axis, including combinations and patient selection markers.
pmc-13319095:
Min Lin and colleagues present a 2026 retrospective study building a prediction chart for partial delirium after heart surgery with a bypass machine. Patients came from one Sichuan hospital between January 2023 and March 2024. Nurses checked for the condition six times daily in intensive care. The cohort held 994 patients.

Partial delirium struck 162 patients, an incidence of 16.30 percent in their count. Nearly half of those later progressed to full delirium. Six factors independently raised risk, including older age and higher body mass index. Pain medication after tube removal carried the largest odds ratio, at 2.918 in their model. Low albumin and low haemoglobin also mattered. The chart's accuracy was moderate, with an area under the curve of 0.744 overall.
pmc-13320395:
Om Prakash Choudhary and Priyanka Choudhary wrote a letter to the editor in 2026 calling for joint infection control at the 2026 FIFA World Cup. The games will draw near six million guests to sixteen host cities spread across three lands, the United States, Canada, and Mexico, with 48 teams in the largest field yet. Dense crowds can seed outbreaks, strain local clinics, and carry germs home across borders.

World guidance urges hosts of huge gatherings to ready public health plans well ahead of time. Risks named run from crowd spread in stadiums and fan zones to surge load on routine care in host cities. A united front among the three host lands, with shared watch systems and fast reply plans, is urged before the first match.
pmc-13320995:
Deepa M. Patel and colleagues evaluate a fellow doctor model for very ill patients stuck in the emergency department in a 2026 study. At one urban referral centre, a second year fellow trained in both emergency and critical care worked in the emergency department for two months. The review mixed staff surveys, work records, and patient outcome data.

Over 26 shifts the fellow met 101 patients waiting for intensive care beds. Among 71 staff who answered the survey, 91.5 percent called the fellow invaluable or very helpful, praising teamwork, faster action, and teaching. The fellow eased 11 moves out of intensive care need and 4 moves into it. Patient stay and discharge outcomes did not differ clearly.
pmc-13322495:
Ramon Cipriano Pacheco de Araújo and colleagues test a swallowing exercise programme in Parkinson's disease in a 2026 pilot trial. Swallowing trouble is common and risky in Parkinson's care. Twenty-six patients were randomised for four weeks of weekly sessions, half doing chin tuck against resistance exercises and half doing a chin down posture method with swallowing practice.

The exercise group improved more on a dysphagia checklist, on maximum tongue pressure, and on a self scored eating tool than the posture group. Cough peak flow did not change clearly in either group. The authors present resistance exercise as the stronger short option for tongue strength and swallowing signs in this small trial.
pmc-13322895:
Linfeng Li introduces a journal collection on type 2 inflammatory skin diseases in a 2026 editorial. Atopic dermatitis is the best known case. New targeted drugs now include antibodies, JAK blockers and PDE-4 blockers. These widen care beyond creams and standard pills.

Reports in the set extend to diseases such as bullous pemphigoid, prurigo nodularis, chronic hives and alopecia areata. The editorial traces how barrier damage lets allergens and microbes in. Alarm signals then drive immune cells to release interleukins and raise IgE levels. One featured study compares biologic drugs and JAK blockers in real-world care in southern Spain. That choice now sits at the heart of clinic practice.
pmc-13324295:
Jingcheng Yu, Yuren Shen and Hao Jia review plant-derived vesicles as therapy platforms, in a 2026 mini-review. Their angle is drug development, not pure biology. These nanoscale sacs come from edible and medicinal plants. They mix natural bioactivity with the scale gains of a natural carrier.

Formation, isolation and testing are compared with mammalian exosomes and synthetic liposomes. Early studies cover bone repair, nerve injury, gut inflammation, cancer and kidney stone disease. The authors weigh dose spread, model limits and mechanism strength in each area. Vesicles also serve as carriers for added drugs. Messy naming and uneven purification are key barriers. Thin drug-tracking data and scarce clinical proof also hold the field back.
pmc-13324495:
Aditya Sidharth and Daesung Shin review how SUMOylation shapes proteins that drive brain disease in a 2026 article. The process attaches a small SUMO protein to target proteins and can steady them or move them within the cell.

Effects differ sharply by disease and by SUMO type. In Alzheimer disease the change steadies harmful proteins, while in progressive supranuclear palsy one form blocks tau removal and another aids it. Added SUMOylation protects cells in stroke and Parkinson disease by clearing toxic proteins. Wrong placement of proteins harms cells in Huntington disease and ALS. The drug TAK-981, which blocks SUMO action, shows early promise in multiple sclerosis and glioblastoma models.
pmc-13325095:
Yosef Knattrup, Andreas Buchgraitz Jensen, and Jonas Elm benchmark quantum chemistry methods for the free energy of air molecule clusters in a 2026 study. New particle formation in the sky drives big climate model uncertainty, and its simulation depends steeply on these energies.

High-level coupled cluster values for 11 monomers and 27 dimers set the reference standard. Common density functionals and composite methods were scored against it, and one pairing, a range-separated functional with a modest basis, erred by just 0.13 kcal per mol on thermal parts. Adding a vibration scaling factor, conformer entropy, and a high-level correction brought results within 1 kcal per mol of measured values. The recipe guides cheaper studies of larger clusters.
pmc-13325795:
Claudia Capurro and colleagues describe a knocked-in front tooth that recovered in an unexpected way in a 2026 dental case report. Traumatic intrusion is among the worst tooth injuries and often ends in root damage or fusion to bone.

A 7-year-old girl arrived with her right upper central incisor driven in by over 10 mm. Surgery repositioned the tooth, a splint held it, and braces then tried to pull it down. Traction failed and neighboring teeth sank instead, raising fears of fusion. Rapid widening of her narrow upper jaw followed for bite reasons. Soon after, the stuck tooth re-erupted on its own. The team treats the link as a hypothesis, not proof.
pmc-13326595:
Caterina Bosio and colleagues explore unmet engagement needs of heart disease patients in Italy in a 2026 qualitative study. People at very high risk often face broken care paths and uneven local access to services.

Five participatory workshops brought together 24 patients and 5 caregivers across four regions. Themes were read against the Patient Health Engagement model across diagnosis, hospital care, discharge, and later adaptation. The move from hospital to home emerged as the most fragile step, with thin guidance and little psychological backing. Weak doctor communication, caregiver strain, and patchy specialist access recurred. Patient associations filled some gaps.
pmc-13327395:
Chia-Liang Wu wrote a 2026 letter to the editor about a rare blood problem tied to a long-acting antipsychotic shot. A 73-year-old man with schizophrenia had taken aripiprazole pills for over two years, then switched to monthly injections of 400 mg to help adherence. Nine months later his hemoglobin had fallen sharply.

Checks of blood, stool, gut, and scans found no bleeding or other clear cause, though his young red cell count was low at 0.3 percent against a normal range starting at 0.5 percent. Transfusions helped only briefly, so the injections, the sole recent change, were blamed and stopped. The case warns doctors to watch blood counts after switching patients to the long-acting form.
pmc-13327495:
Mutaz Mohamed Tageldein and colleagues review rehabilitation after repair of medial meniscus root tears in a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis. Surgery pulls the torn root back through a shin bone tunnel, but programs for weight bearing and movement afterward vary widely. The team gathered study-level program details and patient score changes.

Searches through early 2026 found 31 studies, with 17 pooled, and scores improved a lot after surgery, including a 28.5 point mean gain on a standard knee score and a 34.6 point drop in pain scores on their scales. Results held up under different assumptions for missing data. Comparing programs across studies helps surgeons judge which limits on bending and loading sit well with recovery.
pmc-13328095:
Reshmi Dassaye and a large team track COVID-19 antibodies in a South African school community in a 2026 study. Learners, parents, and teachers at a semi-rural primary school gave samples in May to August 2023 and again in October 2023. Testing used a rapid IgG and IgM kit, adjusted for test accuracy. The group held 292 people, most of them learners.

At the first round, adjusted IgG prevalence sat at 78 percent overall, highest in teachers at 99 percent on the adjusted figure. By follow-up it climbed to 95 percent overall. Learners rose from 74 to 90 percent unadjusted. Silent spread had clearly swept the school community, informing how schools plan for future waves.
pmc-13328495:
Qilian Xia and co-authors set out a trial of electrical acupoint stimulation for nerve pain after breast surgery in a 2026 protocol. Damage to the intercostobrachial nerve brings lasting numbness and burning pain from armpit to inner arm, plus stiff shoulders, and standard care lacks a nerve-repair routine. The planned trial runs at a traditional medicine hospital in Yunnan.

Two hundred patients will be randomized evenly to real or sham stimulation starting the first day after surgery, given every other day. The method joins acupuncture points with skin-level electric pulses and may help axons regrow and rewrap, early work hints. Pain, feeling, shoulder movement, and safety will judge whether the gentle method earns routine use.
pmc-13329795:
Concepcion Padilla and a large team test whether thinking scores can flag who with mild impairment will develop dementia in a 2026 study. The group drew 349 patients from the SPIN cohort who had broad baseline testing between 2009 and 2021 and later follow-up visits. Composite scores covered several thinking domains.

Over 3 years, 37.8 percent of patients moved to dementia in the reported follow-up, while most stayed stable. Those who converted were older and scored lower across all domains at baseline. A tuned model sorted risk well, with repeat checks naming age, sex, schooling, and memory and planning scores as steady predictors. Right-call rates for ruling out and ruling in decline are detailed by the authors for clinic use.
pmc-13329895:
Vimal Ramanuj and co-authors model gas flow and transfer inside hollow fibre bundles for gas separation in a 2026 study. Such modules clean gases by letting chosen gases pass through fibre walls. The team studied bundle-scale flow, where uneven channels and direction effects shape how well gases move and separate.

Results show a trade-off between purity and recovery, the authors report. Smaller fibres give more surface area and higher purity, yet gases reach less deeply into tight bundles, which hurts overall performance. Measures such as a permeability tensor and Sherwood number capture the direction effects. The authors highlight settings where gains balance best. Better bundle design could cut losses and pressure needs in plant-scale modules.
pmc-13330695:
K Jonsson and colleagues survey hands-on skill practice among nursing students in Scandinavia in a 2026 study. Students from Denmark, Norway, and Sweden answered a questionnaire in 2023 about placements. In total, 706 students reported how often they performed core skills, from breathing and circulation care to medication tasks.

Practice rates ran low and uneven across all study years and skill areas in the reported results. Supervision was mostly at hand, yet some skills lacked enough preceptor input. Gaps spanned basic daily care as well as drug tasks. The authors warn that thin practice may weaken readiness for real wards. Placement planning needs firmer guarantees for core skills, they argue.
pmc-13331795:
Clark Mbou-Boutambe and colleagues surveyed rodents across 11 rural sites in Gabon for 2026 work on Trypanosoma lewisi, a rat parasite that has spread worldwide with its hosts. They screened 528 rodents with a gene test aimed at the wider Herpetosoma group.

Parasite DNA turned up at every site, in 56.6 percent of animals overall, and in the invasive black rat at rates from 21.6 to 85.7 percent across home-area sites. A few native species also tested positive, one at 100 percent in a small sample. Sequencing a long gene fragment from 21 positive samples showed all belonged to the T. lewisi subgroup known as genotype AF05b. The authors say invasive rats likely amplify these parasites in Gabon and should be watched as a possible source of human infection.
pmc-13332795:
Xingwei You and Zhongwei Guo review brain imaging evidence on apathy in Alzheimer's disease in a 2026 review. Apathy, a loss of goal-directed drive, is the most common behavioral symptom of the disease. It burdens caregivers heavily, and it is now thought to rest on its own brain biology rather than trailing memory decline.

Across imaging studies published up to 2025, the review locates the core fault in the prefrontal and basal ganglia motivation circuit. Shrinkage and low activity in the anterior cingulate and orbitofrontal cortex track with failed reward weighing, while dorsolateral prefrontal damage fits planning problems. pmc-13333295:
Rezan Bakır and colleagues built a benchmark dataset in 2026 for teaching machines to predict hydrogen output from a light-driven chemical process. Clean hydrogen from photocatalysis is promising, but conditions interact in tangled ways and are hard to model from theory alone.

At Sivas University of Science and Technology, the team ran controlled batch reactor experiments. They used a graphene-supported lanthanum ferrite catalyst and sucrose solution as the helper chemical, measuring evolved hydrogen by gas chromatography. A Box–Behnken design varied solution pH, catalyst strength, and starting hydrogen peroxide strength in a structured grid. The result is 1,370 data points, each tying one input combination to its hydrogen yield, released through Kaggle with raw and scaled versions plus heatmaps and importance charts. The authors present it as the first shared benchmark for AI models in this kind of photocatalysis.
pmc-13333395:
Shihui Li and colleagues show in a 2026 immunology study that boosting one small protein helps killer T cells endure the long grind of chronic infection. Constant antigen exposure usually exhausts CD8 T cells, and keeping a working pool of them has been an unsolved problem for therapy design.

pmc-13333695:

Cultures were positive in 41 cases, most often growing Cutibacterium acnes, Staphylococcus aureus, or Streptococcus intermedius. IV antibiotics ran a median of six weeks, and some patients needed repeat surgery. At a median follow-up of 11 months, about two-thirds of survivors with full data reached a good working outcome. The decade of work offers hands-on guidance on germs, treatment length, and likely recovery.
pmc-13337095:
Weitong Gao and colleagues trace lung cancer immunotherapy resistance to a missing RNA editor in a 2026 study. Tumors lacking RBM10 built a suppressive setting rich in M2 macrophages, the calm, tumor-helping type. The loss warped splicing of the sensor STING, shifting its form balance.

pmc-13337395:
Yuan Liu and a large team test whether psychological distress raises thyroid cancer risk in a 2026 UK Biobank cohort study. The results tie mental health to cancer risk partly through metabolic paths.
pmc-13339895:
Meshack Tweya Omwega and colleagues systematically build three-phage cocktails against drug-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa in a 2026 study. Single phages invite resistance, and cocktails are usually mixed by guesswork. A combinatorial method tested interactions directly on clinical isolates.

Only one triple acted in synergy, reaching 84.1 percent inhibition, while half the triples clashed.
pmc-13341295:
LED lighting shapes both the nutrition and safety of microgreens, according to a 2026 review by Anushuya Guragain and coauthors. Microgreens are young seedlings packed with micronutrients, usually raised indoors where light spectrum, intensity, and day length can be tuned precisely.

Studies show these light settings shift growth, yield, and nutrient content, though results vary by species and most work covers the Brassicaceae family. Photoperiod remains barely studied. A bigger gap concerns microbes: pathogens can persist on microgreens, yet almost no research tracks their survival under LED systems during production or storage. The authors call for full food safety protocols built around LED growing.
pmc-13341595:
A protective gene shared by two inflammatory diseases is identified by Qinjin Dai and colleagues in a 2026 integrative study. Behçet's disease and inflammatory bowel disease overlap clinically, so the team combined single-cell blood data with genetic causal inference to hunt common targets.

Mendelian randomization singled out BTN3A2 as protective in both conditions, and its genetic signals aligned spatially with disease risk signals. Validation ran through a mouse eye inflammation model, outside datasets, and patient blood samples, strengthening the case for a shared treatment target.
pmc-13347395:
Asmaa M. Arafa and colleagues grow an endangered henbane in tissue culture to raise its drug alkaloids, in a study from 2026. Egyptian Hyoscyamus albus makes scopolamine and hyoscyamine that are hard to build in a lab. So callus and hairy root cultures were fed zinc oxide in plain and nano forms at varied doses, and extracts were profiled by gas methods.

Hairy roots beat the parent plant for scopolamine output, and culture-only tropinone appeared in the profiles in the reported scans. Plain zinc oxide led atropine gains in callus, while nano and plain forms split the lead for roots and their medium. Extracts also fought microbes and curbed their virulence traits.
pmc-13347695:
Clara Davoine, Gaël Cobraiville, Lionel Pochet, and Marianne Fillet measure drug binding on tiny membrane sacs taken from cancer cells, in a methods study published in 2026. Golgi sacs keep membrane proteins in near-native settings, yet binding there is hard to read. Tests centred on UGCG, a Golgi protein of cancer interest, using fairly even sacs near 150 nm across that kept native inner structure in the reported checks. pmc-13348195:
Jean-Pierre Fina-Lubaki, Williams R. Phillips, and Klaus B. von Pressentin introduce a French edition of a primary care reporting checklist, in an editorial from 2026. Primary care has its own methods, patients, and system settings, so the CRISP checklist was built by global consensus to lift quality, relevance. Openness in reports across number, story, and mixed study types alike.

French spans the globe, above all in Africa, yet English rules science publishing and shuts out many French-speaking researchers from sharing work clearly. A French checklist serves authors, reviewers, editors, teachers, and planners, easing entry and helping readers judge and apply findings in Francophone care settings.
pmc-13349395:
Chen Chen, Hao Wu, and Lei Zhang link coaching style to athlete burnout. Their survey study appeared in 2026. It covers college athletes in China. Basic mental needs sit at the centre. Questionnaires came from 800 student athletes. Modelling ran in two stages. A structural model came first. A neural network check came second. Coaching was sorted into two styles. One style gives autonomy. The other style controls. Three needs were tracked throughout. They are autonomy, competence, and closeness.

Supportive coaching tied to lower burnout. Controlling coaching tied to higher burnout. All three needs carried part of each link. Competence carried the strongest share. The autonomy path ran clearer in female athletes. That path runs from supportive coaching to burnout. Coaches can cut burnout by feeding needs. Merely easing training load is not the lesson.
pmc-13349895:
Xiangqiong Wu and fellow authors proposed a lightweight detection system in 2026 for finding breast lesions in ultrasound images. Ultrasound is cheap and safe, but speckle noise, low contrast, and fuzzy lesion borders make automatic reading hard.

Built on a YOLOv13 detector, their design adds a module that gathers wide image context and another that follows horizontal and vertical structure, placed at chosen stages to keep costs low. On two datasets it reached strong detection results with only 2.50 million parameters and fast processing. Extra tests for robustness and cross-dataset use supported the design. A small, quick model like this could fit clinics without heavy computing power.
pmc-13350195:
S. Gogia and a Houston team described in 2026 how a multidisciplinary programme supports infant feeding choices for parents living with HIV across a national guideline change. Newer guidance backs shared decision making, and their centre built a team model in 2020 ahead of that shift.

Records covered 336 parents entering care between 2020 and 2025. Seventy-five considered breastfeeding, 51 took a specialist consultation, and 37 breastfed, with no transmissions recorded and most keeping the virus undetectable, for a median of 47 days. The experience shows a structured, team-based conversation can safely support parents who choose to breastfeed.
pmc-13351095:
Qilin Shu and colleagues tracked microbes and chemistry together as a traditional Chinese medicine starter ferments, in a 2026 study. The process reshapes the active parts of Hua Feng Dan, but which microbes do the work was unclear.

Sixty flavonoids shifted notably during the process, with catechin and naringin rising while many others fell. Bacteria such as Tetragenococcus and Bacillus led at different stages, and the fungus Aspergillus was also prominent. Two strains were tied to ten of the flavonoid changes. Re-running the process with those two strains raised the total flavonoid level a lot, so makers could steer quality on purpose instead of leaving it to chance.
pmc-13351395:
Atefeh Valaei and co-authors reviewed gut microbes in blood cancers in a 2026 narrative review. It covered evidence from 2022 to 2025. Gut microbes help keep immunity balanced. They support blood cell growth. They also release active compounds such as short-chain fatty acids.

When that ecosystem is disturbed, blood cancers may grow faster. These include leukaemias, lymphomas, and myeloma. Infections grow likelier, and treatment grows harder to bear. Chemotherapy, antibiotics, and stem cell transplants in turn batter the microbes. The review maps this two-way relationship mechanism by mechanism. Guarding or restoring gut microbes is emerging as a support strategy beside standard treatment.
pmc-13351695:
Ebtihal Elameen Eltyeb leads a 2026 systematic review of regenerative medicine for children with cerebral palsy. Current care mainly manages symptoms, while cell-based approaches aim to support brain repair and better function. Four databases were searched for work from 2010 to 2025, covering trials, cohort studies, and case series with at least three children.

Eighteen studies with 1,087 children were analysed, and most used products drawn from umbilical cord tissue or blood. Cord-based treatments showed moderate motor gains in selected trials. Combined cord blood with erythropoietin gave the largest motor and thinking gains in the set. Because study designs differed widely, results were combined in words rather than pooled numbers.
pmc-13351895:
Fahad Idrees Shaikh and co-authors report a 2026 case of an ancient schwannoma on the cervical sympathetic chain in the neck. Such slow, benign nerve sheath tumours develop wear-like changes over time that can look like cancer. A 53-year-old man had a painless swelling below his left ear for six months.

Scans suggested a dead lymph node in the neck, and a needle sample gave too few cells to judge. Surgeons removed the mass fully, and tissue study confirmed the ancient schwannoma diagnosis. Horner syndrome followed surgery and was managed without further procedures. The case stresses tissue proof and careful planning for nerve risks before neck surgery.
pmc-13353795:
Karen Sanchez-Tamayo and co-authors report pressure alopecia in a young child in 2026. The hair loss type follows long immobilisation and is seen mostly in adults, with few child cases known. A four-year-old patient developed a bare patch after a two-week intensive care stay.

Scope exam of the scalp showed comedone-like dots that supported the diagnosis. After two months of steroids and zinc pyrithione shampoo, signs of scarring hair loss still appeared. Early suspicion after long hospital or surgical immobilisation is vital, since most cases recover on their own but scarring can be permanent.
pmc-13354395:
Muhammad Farhan leads a 2026 pooled analysis of rivaroxaban plus aspirin versus aspirin alone in peripheral artery disease. Aspirin is the base drug, yet clot risk stays high in the narrowed-leg-artery disease. Trials following PRISMA guidance were pooled with random-effects models, with bias and certainty graded by standard tools.

pmc-13354995:
A 2026 proceedings volume gathers abstracts from the International Congress on Academic Medicine, held in Ottawa from April 16 to 19. The meeting, run by the Association of Faculties of Medicine of Canada, drew more than 1,900 people. Attendees included students, residents, teachers, researchers, and patient partners from many countries.

Sessions covered health falsehoods, kindness in care, food and child health, and the health of the planet, alongside workshops and poster talks. pmc-13357095:
Junjie Liu and co-authors built in 2026 a relapse prediction chart for HER2-positive breast cancer treated with trastuzumab, a targeted drug some tumors learn to resist. pmc-13358995:
Eun-Jeong Seo and co-authors map collagen genes in scarred lungs in a 2026 study. Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis stiffens the lungs as too much matrix builds up between air sacs. Cells called fibroblasts lay down that matrix, chiefly collagens. Two collagen types are well known culprits, but the full family had not been charted in these cells.

pmc-13359695:
Vimal Murugesan and co-authors survey the modern treatment of melanoma in a 2026 review. This aggressive skin cancer was once nearly hopeless once it spread. Surgery still cures early disease. Newer options grow a patient's own tumor-attacking immune cells and return them, or use viruses that attack the tumor. pmc-13361295:
Oliver Planz reviews how cancer drugs that block a signal enzyme affect the immune system's alarms in a 2026 paper. pmc-13361395:

The team sorted the helps and hurdles into levels, starting with the evidence itself. Knowing where the friction sits, in habits, staffing, or supply, tells managers what to fix first so proven care actually reaches patients.
pmc-13362395:

pmc-13362595:

pmc-13363695:

pmc-13364695:

pmc-13365295:

pmc-13366095:

pmc-13369795:

pmc-13372195:

pmc-13372695:

pmc-13373295:

pmc-13374195:

pmc-13375895:

pmc-13376795:

pmc-13377595:

pmc-13378495:

pmc-13379995:

pmc-13380095:

pmc-13380195:

pmc-13386395:

pmc-13386495:

Only a minority of units could reliably flag patients needing screening or track carriers by computer. Under a third assigned dedicated caregivers to carriers, and rules for lifting precautions varied widely. Staff chiefly blamed missing national dialysis-specific guidance and poor flow of carrier status information between services.
pmc-13388495:

pmc-13389095:

pmc-13392195:
